Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 37, verses 1–7:

(p-270) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat al-Saffat (the Rows)

It is Meccan, and its count in the Medinan, Syrian and Kufan reckonings is one hundred and eighty-two verses.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿By those who range in ranks,﴾ ﴿and those who drive with a driving,﴾ ﴿and those who recite the reminder,﴾ ﴿indeed your God is One,﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and Lord of the easts.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment of the stars,﴾ ﴿and as a protection against every rebellious devil.﴾

Allah, exalted is He, swears in these verses by things from among His creatures, and people differed about their meaning. Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq and Qatadah said: they are the angels who are arranged in rows in the heaven in the worship and remembrance of Allah, exalted is He. A group said: He intended everyone among the children of Adam who is arranged in rows in battle in the cause of Allah, or in prayer and obedience, and the implied meaning is: "by the ranks that range" (al-jama'at al-saffat). The wording may encompass all of these things mentioned.

"Those who drive with a driving": Mujahid and al-Suddi said: they are the angels who drive the clouds and other creatures of Allah. Qatadah said: they are the verses of the Qur'an that contain the legal prohibitions.

His saying, ﴿and those who recite the reminder﴾, means: those who recite. Mujahid and al-Suddi said: He intended the angels who recite His remembrance. Qatadah said: He intended the children of Adam who recite His revealed books, and His glorification and magnification, and the like.

Abu 'Amr and Hamza recited [wal-saffati saffa] with idgham (assimilation, merging the consonants), and this is the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, (p-271) Masruq and al-A'mash. The rest of the readers and the majority of people recited with izhar (clear pronunciation, without merging), and likewise in all of them. Abu Hatim said: "Izhar is our preference." As for "al-hamilati wiqra" (those who carry a load) and "al-jariyati yusra" (those who run with ease), idgham is not permissible in them, because the ta' is distant from the two letters.

Then He, exalted is He, clarified what is sworn to: that it is His Oneness, and that He is one, meaning: unified in all the aspects from which the thinker considers. Then He, exalted is He, described Himself with His lordship over all creatures, and mentioned "the easts" (al-mashariq), because they are the places where lights rise, and the eyes are more strained by them, and in mentioning them there is sufficiency from mentioning the wests (al-maghárib), since their correspondence to them is understood by every person of intellect. Blessed and exalted is He intended the risings of the sun, which are one hundred and eighty in the year according to what they claim, from the longest day of the year to its shortest. Then He informed of His power in adorning the heaven with the stars, and included in that adornment that He made them a protection and a guard from the rebellious devils, who are those who eavesdrop on the hearing.

The majority read "adornment" (zinah) in construct with "the stars" (al-kawakib). Hamza and Hafs from 'Asim read with tanwin on (zinatin) and khafd on (al-kawakibi) as an apposition to it; this is the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq (according to a variant from him), Abu Zur'ah ibn 'Umar ibn Jarir, Ibn Wathab and Talhah. Abu Bakr from 'Asim read: "bi-zinatin" with tanwin, [al-kawakiba] with fath, and this is the recitation of Ibn Wathab, Abu 'Amr, al-A'mash and Masruq. This, in terms of grammatical analysis (i'rab), is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger﴾ [al-Balad: 14] ﴿an orphan near of kin﴾ [al-Balad: 15]. Al-Zahrawi transmitted a reading with tanwin on "zinatin" and raf' on "al-kawakibu".

"Al-marid" (the rebellious one): the one stripped bare for evil; from it comes "a barren tree" (shajarah mardá'), meaning one without leaves on it, and from it comes "al-amrad" (the beardless youth). Allah, exalted is He, singled out the nearest heaven for mention because it is the one that meets our sight directly, and also because protection from the devil exists in it alone. "Hifzan" (as a protection) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), and it was said: it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), and the waw is extra.

It is Meccan, and its count in the Medinan, Syrian and Kufan reckonings is one hundred and eighty-two verses.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿By those who range in ranks,﴾ ﴿and those who drive with a driving,﴾ ﴿and those who recite the reminder,﴾ ﴿indeed your God is One,﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and Lord of the easts.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment of the stars,﴾ ﴿and as a protection against every rebellious devil.﴾

Allah, exalted is He, swears in these verses by things from among His creatures, and people differed about their meaning. Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq and Qatadah said: they are the angels who are arranged in rows in the heaven in the worship and remembrance of Allah, exalted is He. A group said: He intended everyone among the children of Adam who is arranged in rows in battle in the cause of Allah, or in prayer and obedience, and the implied meaning is: "by the ranks that range" (al-jama'at al-saffat). The wording may encompass all of these things mentioned.

"Those who drive with a driving": Mujahid and al-Suddi said: they are the angels who drive the clouds and other creatures of Allah. Qatadah said: they are the verses of the Qur'an that contain the legal prohibitions.

His saying, ﴿and those who recite the reminder﴾, means: those who recite. Mujahid and al-Suddi said: He intended the angels who recite His remembrance. Qatadah said: He intended the children of Adam who recite His revealed books, and His glorification and magnification, and the like.

Abu 'Amr and Hamza recited [wal-saffati saffa] with idgham (assimilation, merging the consonants), and this is the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, (p-271) Masruq and al-A'mash. The rest of the readers and the majority of people recited with izhar (clear pronunciation, without merging), and likewise in all of them. Abu Hatim said: "Izhar is our preference." As for "al-hamilati wiqra" (those who carry a load) and "al-jariyati yusra" (those who run with ease), idgham is not permissible in them, because the ta' is distant from the two letters.

Then He, exalted is He, clarified what is sworn to: that it is His Oneness, and that He is one, meaning: unified in all the aspects from which the thinker considers. Then He, exalted is He, described Himself with His lordship over all creatures, and mentioned "the easts" (al-mashariq), because they are the places where lights rise, and the eyes are more strained by them, and in mentioning them there is sufficiency from mentioning the wests (al-maghárib), since their correspondence to them is understood by every person of intellect. Blessed and exalted is He intended the risings of the sun, which are one hundred and eighty in the year according to what they claim, from the longest day of the year to its shortest. Then He informed of His power in adorning the heaven with the stars, and included in that adornment that He made them a protection and a guard from the rebellious devils, who are those who eavesdrop on the hearing.

The majority read "adornment" (zinah) in construct with "the stars" (al-kawakib). Hamza and Hafs from 'Asim read with tanwin on (zinatin) and khafd on (al-kawakibi) as an apposition to it; this is the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq (according to a variant from him), Abu Zur'ah ibn 'Umar ibn Jarir, Ibn Wathab and Talhah. Abu Bakr from 'Asim read: "bi-zinatin" with tanwin, [al-kawakiba] with fath, and this is the recitation of Ibn Wathab, Abu 'Amr, al-A'mash and Masruq. This, in terms of grammatical analysis (i'rab), is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger﴾ [al-Balad: 14] ﴿an orphan near of kin﴾ [al-Balad: 15]. Al-Zahrawi transmitted a reading with tanwin on "zinatin" and raf' on "al-kawakibu".

"Al-marid" (the rebellious one): the one stripped bare for evil; from it comes "a barren tree" (shajarah mardá'), meaning one without leaves on it, and from it comes "al-amrad" (the beardless youth). Allah, exalted is He, singled out the nearest heaven for mention because it is the one that meets our sight directly, and also because protection from the devil exists in it alone. "Hifzan" (as a protection) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), and it was said: it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), and the waw is extra.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 37, verses 8–10:**

Allah the Exalted says:

﴿They cannot listen to the exalted assembly, and they are pelted from every side,﴾ ﴿repelled, and theirs is a constant punishment,﴾ ﴿except one who snatches a snatch, and a piercing flame pursues him.﴾

"Al-mala' al-a'la" (the exalted assembly): the inhabitants of the lowest heaven and what is above it. All of them are called "a'la" (exalted) in relation to the assembly of the earth, which is lower. The pronoun in "yassamma'una" refers to the devils (shayatin).

The majority of reciters and people read "yasma'una" with a sukun on the sin and a light mim. Hamza, 'Asim (in the transmission of Hafs), Ibn 'Abbas (with a variant reported from him), Ibn Wuthab, 'Abdullah ibn Muslim, Talha, and al-A'mash read "la yassamma'una" with a shaddah on both the sin and the mim, meaning "they do not eavesdrop" (la yatasamma'una). On the first reading, their hearing is negated, even if they do listen. This is the sound meaning, and it is supported by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, they are removed from hearing.﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:212]. On the last reading, any listening or hearing on their part is negated. The apparent meaning of the reports is that they still listen, but they do not hear. If any of them hears something, he does not escape before he passes that hearing to the one who comes to him. This is because, since the time of Muhammad (ﷺ), the sky has been filled with strong guards and meteors, whereas the stoning in the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic era of ignorance) was lighter. Authentic hadiths (ahadith sihah, prophetic reports) have been narrated on this subject, the content of which is: "The devils used to ascend to the sky and sit in positions for eavesdropping, one above another. The one closest to the sky would go first, then the one after him. Allah the Exalted would decree a matter concerning the earth, and the inhabitants of the sky would discuss it. The lowest devil would hear it from them and pass it to the one beneath him. Sometimes a meteor would burn him before he had cast the word, and sometimes he would not be burned before he had passed the whole sentence. He would then convey that word to the soothsayers (kuhhan), and they would add a hundred lies to it. The word would come true, and the ignorant would believe all of it." When Allah the Exalted brought Islam, the sky was guarded with great severity, and no devil who listened ever escaped entirely. It is also reported that they do not hear anything now.

The "al-kawakib al-rajimah" (the stoning stars) are those which people see shooting down. Al-Naqqash and Makki said: they are not the stars that move through the sky, because the motion of those is not seen, whereas the motion of these stoning stars is seen because they are close to us. There is room for examination in this. "Yuqdhafun" means: they are stoned (yurjamun).

"Al-duhur" (repulsion): disgrace and humiliation, because "al-zajr" is pushing away with force. Mujahid said: "driven away." The majority read "duhuran" with a damma on the dal. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "dahuran" with a fatha on the dal. "Al-wasib" means "the constant," as said by Mujahid, Qatadah, and 'Ikrimah. Al-Suddi and Abu Salih said: "al-wasib" means "the painful," and from it comes "al-wasb" (illness, affliction). The meaning is that this is the prevailing condition of all the devils, except one who deviates and snatches a report or news, and a meteor pursues him and burns him.

The majority of people read "khatifa" with a fatha on the kha' and a kasra on the ta', lightly. Al-Hasan and Qatadah read "khittifa" with a kasra on the kha' and the ta', with a shaddah on the ta'. Abu Hatim said: this is the dialect of Bakr ibn Wa'il and Tamim ibn Murra. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he read it with a kasra on the kha' and the ta', lightly. "Al-thaqib" means that which pierces through with its light and its bright ray, as said by Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd. And "hasab thaqib" is used when lineage is noble and radiant.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 37, verses 11–18:

(p-274) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿So ask them: are they the more difficult to create, or those We have created? Indeed We created them from sticky clay.﴾ ﴿But you marvel, and they mock.﴾ ﴿And when they are reminded, they do not remember.﴾ ﴿And when they see a sign, they mock it.﴾ ﴿And they say: This is nothing but manifest magic.﴾ ﴿When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised again?﴾ ﴿And our forefathers, the earlier ones?﴾ ﴿Say: Yes, and you will be humbled.﴾

Al-istifta' (asking for a ruling) is a type of question, as if it were the question of one whose words are taken as authoritative and made into proof. Likewise, their statements in this verse are such that they cannot say anything but that the creation of others besides them, of the nations, the angels, mankind and jinn, the heavens, the earth, the easts and other things, is more difficult than these addressees. And the pronoun in "[khalaqna]" (We created) refers to what was mentioned earlier. Mujahid, Qatadah and others said: in the Codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: [am min 'adadna] (or of those We counted), meaning from the ranks (al-Saffat) and others, and the heavens, the earth and what is between them. Likewise al-A'mash recited "amman" with a light mim, without "am".

Then He, exalted, informed with a definite statement about His creation of Adam, who is the father of mankind, and attributed the creation from clay to all people, since the father was created from it. Al-Tabari said: He created Adam from earth, water, fire and air, and all of this, when mixed, becomes sticky clay (tin lazib), that is, what clings (al-lazim): it adheres to what is near it and sticks to it, and it is like the dry clay (al-salsal) like pottery. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah explained "lazib" as "noble" (al-hurr), that is, the excellent and fine, but the real meaning is what we have mentioned. It is said: darba lazib and lazim with the same meaning.

The majority recited: ﴿"'ajibta"﴾ with a fatha on the ta', that is, O Muhammad, at their turning away from the truth and their blindness to guidance, and that they should be disbelievers despite what you have brought them from Allah. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited with a damma on the ta', and it is related from 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Wathhab, al-Nakha'i, Talhah, Sufyan, and al-A'mash, and this is on the basis that He, exalted, is the one who marvels. The meaning of this from Allah, glorified is He, is that it is an attribute of action, like His, upon him be prayer and peace, saying: "Allah marvels at a people who are led to Paradise in chains," (p-275) and His saying: "Allah marvels at the young man who has no inclination (to sin)." These are only expressions of what He manifests in one aspect of Himself. So the meaning of this verse is: Rather I marvel at their misguidance and the evil of their creed, and I have made it a matter of marvel for those who look at it and at what accompanies it of My law and My guidance. It is related from Shurayh that he denied this reading, and said: Indeed Allah does not marvel. Al-A'mash said: I mentioned that to Ibrahim, and he said: Shurayh was pleased with his own knowledge, and 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) is more knowledgeable than him. Makki and 'Ali ibn Sulayman in the book of al-Zahrawi said: it is a report from the Prophet ﷺ about himself, as if he said: "Say to them: I marvel." His saying: ﴿"and they mock"﴾ means: while they mock your prophethood and the truth that you have.

His, exalted, saying: ﴿"yastaskhirun"﴾ means: by the sign, which is the proof and the indication. It is related that it was revealed concerning Rukanah, a Meccan polytheist man, who met the Prophet ﷺ on a barren mountain while he was tending his sheep, and he was the strongest person of his time. He said to him: "O Rukanah, if I wrestle you down, will you believe in me?" He said: "Yes." So he threw him down three times. Then he showed him signs of a tree calling and coming to him, and similar things, in which the wording of the hadith varies. When he finished all of that, he did not believe, and went to Mecca and said: "O Banu Hashim, your companion has bewitched the people of the earth!" So the verse was revealed concerning him and his likes. "Yastaskhirun" means: they seek to be among those who mock; and it may mean "yaskhar" (they mock), like His saying: ﴿"and Allah is self-sufficient"﴾ [al-Taghabun: 6], so that fa'ala and istaf'ala have the same meaning. Mujahid and Qatadah explained it this way. In some earlier readings: "yastashirun" with an unpointed ha', and this is an expression of what Rukanah said, since he sought to make him a sorcerer, upon him be prayer and peace.

His, exalted, saying: ﴿"a-idha mitna"﴾. Abu Ja'far, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and the general readers recited with a damma on the mim, and al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Shaybah and Nafi' recited with a kasra. Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and Nafi' recited "aw aba'una" with a sukun on the waw, and it is the waw of division or choice. The majority recited it with a fatha, and it is the waw of conjunction, to which the interrogative alif has been prefixed.

Then He, exalted, commanded him to answer their affirmation with "Yes", and to add to the answer that they, in the resurrection, will be in humiliation and abasement. "Al-dakhir" is the humbled, the abased. The readings of the two interrogatives have been mentioned more than once before.

(p-274) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿So ask them: are they the more difficult to create, or those We have created? Indeed We created them from sticky clay.﴾ ﴿But you marvel, and they mock.﴾ ﴿And when they are reminded, they do not remember.﴾ ﴿And when they see a sign, they mock it.﴾ ﴿And they say: This is nothing but manifest magic.﴾ ﴿When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised again?﴾ ﴿And our forefathers, the earlier ones?﴾ ﴿Say: Yes, and you will be humbled.﴾

Al-istifta' (asking for a ruling) is a type of question, as if it were the question of one whose words are taken as authoritative and made into proof. ﴿Then it will be only a single shout, and behold, they will be looking.﴾ ﴿And they will say, "Woe to us! This is the Day of Recompense."﴾ ﴿"This is the Day of Judgement which you used to deny."﴾ ﴿"Gather those who did wrong, and their companions, and what they used to worship"﴾ ﴿"besides Allah, and guide them to the path of Hellfire."﴾ ﴿"And stop them, for they are to be questioned."﴾ ﴿"What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?"﴾ ﴿"Rather, today they are submitting."﴾

This is a resumptive statement of information, carried on by what precedes it. Allah, exalted is He, informs that He will raise them from their graves: "it will be only a single shout" (zajra wahida), which is the blast of resurrection in the Trumpet (al-Sur). His words ﴿"yanzurun"﴾ (they will be looking) may mean that they look with their eyes, that is, they see their situation and the truth of what they used to deny. It may also mean "they await" (yantazirun), that is, they wait for what will be done to them and what they will be commanded.

Then He informs us that in that state they say: ﴿"Ya waylana"﴾ (Woe to us!). They call out to woe (al-wayl), meaning: this is the time of your arrival and the moment of your descent. Abu Hatim transmitted a pause here and made His words ﴿"This is the Day of Recompense"﴾ part of the speech of Allah or of the angels addressed to them. Others held that the rest of the verse is the speech of the disbelievers. Al-din (recompense) means requital and repayment, as in their saying: "As you do, so will you be repaid." They agreed that His words ﴿"This is the Day of Judgement"﴾ are not the speech of the disbelievers; the meaning is that it is said to them: "This is the Day of Judgement."

His words, exalted is He, ﴿"wa-azwajahum"﴾ (and their companions) mean their kinds (anwa') and their like. This was said by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatada. From the same root is His saying: ﴿"And you were in three kinds"﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 7], and His saying: ﴿"And when souls are joined in pairs"﴾ [al-Takwir: 7], that is, they are grouped by kind. It has been related that at this moment every type is gathered with its own type, and every companion among the disbelievers with his companion. With them is what they used to worship besides Allah, whether a human who was content with that or an idol or a statue, as a rebuke to them and a display of the wretchedness of their condition. Al-Hasan said: the meaning is "and their wives, the polytheistic women," and this was related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them). Al-Rummani preferred this view.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿"fahduhum"﴾ (and guide them) mean: set them straight and drive them onto the path of the Blazing Fire (al-Jahim). Al-Jahim is one of the levels of Hell, said to be the fourth. Then He commands that they be stopped. The verb waqafa is transitive by itself, as you say "I stopped Zayd" (waqaftu Zaydan). His command to stop them is for the purpose of rebuke and questioning. People differed about what they will be questioned about. It was related from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud that he said: they will be asked, "Do you love to drink cold water?" This is a form of mockery toward them. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: they will be asked about "There is no god but Allah." Most of the exegetes said: about their deeds, and they will be made to stand before their ugliness. This is a general view that includes mockery and other things. Anas related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever calls a man to something, that thing will be binding on him," and he recited: ﴿"And stop them, for they are to be questioned."﴾ Ibn Mas'ud related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The feet of a servant will not move from before Allah, exalted is He, until he is asked about five things: about his youth, how he spent it; about his life, how he used it up; about his wealth, how he earned it and how he spent it; and about what he did with what he knew."

In my view, the meaning may also be in line with what He explained by His words ﴿"What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?"﴾, that is, they will be asked about their refusal to help one another. Shayba and Nafi' read it with one ta' (tus'alun, with a single ta' as the verb's first letter), while Khalid read it with two ta's (tatasa'alun), and so did the reading in the codex of 'Abd Allah. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read it with the ta' assimilated into the ta' in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Tha'labi said: this is the answer of Abu Jahl when he said at Badr: ﴿"We are a united army that will be victorious"﴾ [al-Qamar: 44].

Then He, exalted is He, informs us of their answer on that day, in the state of submission and surrender, ﴿"Rather, today they are submitting."﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 37, verse 27–34:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And they will turn to one another, questioning each other.﴾ ﴿They will say, "Indeed, you used to come to us from the right."﴾ ﴿They will say, "Rather, you were not believers."﴾ ﴿And we had over you no authority; rather, you were a transgressing people.﴾ ﴿So the word of our Lord has come into effect against us; indeed, we are going to taste [the punishment].﴾ ﴿So we led you astray; indeed, we were ourselves astray.﴾ ﴿Indeed, they, that Day, will be sharers in the punishment.﴾ ﴿Indeed, that is how We deal with the criminals.﴾

This group, whose members turn to one another, are jinn and humankind. This is the view of Qatadah. Their questioning is by way of reproach, blame and anger. The speakers, "You used to come to us," are either humans speaking to the devils, which is the view of Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, or the weak among humankind speaking to the great ones and leaders. The exegetes have differed over the meaning of their words, ﴿"from the right"﴾. Ibn Zayd expressed it as "the way of Paradise and goodness," and expressions of this kind, which are explained according to meaning, are not restricted to the wording itself. Some of them went in the direction of a specific interpretation of the verse. What results from this are several meanings. Among them: that by "the right" is meant strength and power, so it is as if they said: "You used to mislead us by a strength from you, and lead us onto the path of error by following with vigour." He expressed these meanings by "the right," as the Arabs say: "with two hands he did not bring," and as they say "the hand" in other places to mean strength. Some people have taken the verse of al-Shammakh in this direction, namely his saying:

؎ When a banner is raised for glory, ∗∗∗ ʿUrabah receives it with the right.

They said: its meaning is "with strength and determination," for otherwise everyone would receive it with his right hand if it were the limb, and also, he only used the banner as a metaphor for glory, so likewise he did not mean the limb by "the right."

Among the meanings the verse may bear is that they mean: "You used to come to us from the direction which your deception and misleading make appear good, and in which it appears to be the direction of guidance and rightness, so it becomes for us like the right, by which we seek good omen from the bird that comes to us from its side." It is as if they likened the words of these misleaders to the auspicious omens which they regard as praiseworthy, as though the deception in these seductions had made appear in them what is about to be praised.

Among the meanings the verse may bear is that they mean: "You used to come to us," that is, you would cut us off from news of good and the right, so he expressed this by "the right," since the right is the direction by which one seeks blessing, and by everything in it and from it.

Among the meanings the verse may bear is that they mean: "You used to come to us from the direction of desires and lack of reflection." The heavy side of a human is the right, because his liver is in it, and his left side has his heart in it, and it is lighter. This is the meaning of the poet's words:

؎ We left them the left side.

That is, we gave way to them on the path of flight, because the one who is defeated only retreats on his left side, as it is the lighter of his two sides. Since the human heart is on the left and his sight is there, it is as though these people used to come from the direction of desires and heaviness. This interpretation is most fitting with the seduction of the devils, and it is strained with the seduction of the sons of Adam.

(p-280) It was said: the meaning is: they swear to us and come to us in the manner of one whom, if he swears to us, we believe him. So "the right," according to this, is the oath.

Some people, in explaining Iblis's mention of the directions of the sons of Adam in His saying: ﴿from before them and from behind them and from their right and from their left﴾ [al-A'raf: 17], went to what we have mentioned about the direction of desires, and said: "What is before them is his deceiving them in what they see; what is behind them is his stealing upon them in secret; from their right is the side of their desires; and from their left is their sight with the heart, and his warning, for the devil may overcome him in it." This applies to those who take them as the specific directions of the son of Adam, and some of them took them as the directions of his affairs and concerns, so the interpretation is broader on this view.

Then God, exalted is He, related the saying of the jinn answering these people: ﴿Rather, you were not believers﴾ as you claimed; rather, you had acquired disbelief and insight into it. We only led you to what we ourselves were led to, and there was no proof or power for us over you except your transgression and your will for disbelief. So the word has come into effect upon all of us, and the punishment has become binding on us, and indeed we are all going to taste it. Tasting here is a metaphor, and it is in this manner that Qatadah and others explained that it is the saying of the jinn up to ﴿astray﴾.

Then God, exalted is He, informed that they all shared in the punishment and were gathered in it, and that this is His treatment of the people of crime, who accumulate sin and disbelief.

The exegetes have differed over the meaning of their words, ﴿"from the right"﴾. Ibn Zayd expressed it as "the way of Paradise and goodness," and expressions of this kind, which are explained according to meaning, are not restricted to the wording itself. Some of them went in the direction of a specific interpretation of the verse. What results from this are several meanings. Among them: that by "the right" is meant strength and power, so it is as if they said: "You used to mislead us by a strength from you, and lead us onto the path of error by following with vigour." He expressed these meanings by "the right," as the Arabs say: "with two hands he did not bring," and as they say "the hand" in other places to mean strength. Some people have taken the verse of al-Shammakh in this direction, namely his saying:

؎ When a banner is raised for glory, ∗∗∗ ʿUrabah receives it with the right.

They said: its meaning is "with strength and determination," for otherwise everyone would receive it with his right hand if it were the limb, and also, he only used the banner as a metaphor for glory, so likewise he did not mean the limb by "the right."

Among the meanings the verse may bear is that they mean: "You used to come to us from the direction which your deception and misleading make appear good, and in which it appears to be the direction of guidance and rightness, so it becomes for us like the right, by which we seek good omen from the bird that comes to us from its side." It is as if they likened the words of these misleaders to the auspicious omens which they regard as praiseworthy, as though the deception in these seductions had made appear in them what is about to be praised.

Among the meanings the verse may bear is that they mean: "You used to come to us," that is, you would cut us off from news of good and the right, so he expressed this by "the right," since the right is the direction by which one seeks blessing, and by everything in it and from it.

Among the meanings the verse may bear is that they mean: "You used to come to us from the direction of desires and lack of reflection." The heavy side of a human is the right, because his liver is in it, and his left side has his heart in it, and it is lighter. This is the meaning of the poet's words:

؎ We left them the left side.

That is, we gave way to them on the path of flight, because the one who is defeated only retreats on his left side, as it is the lighter of his two sides. Since the human heart is on the left and his sight is there, it is as though these people used to come from the direction of desires and heaviness. This interpretation is most fitting with the seduction of the devils, and it is strained with the seduction of the sons of Adam.

(p-280) It was said: the meaning is: they swear to us and come to us in the manner of one whom, if he swears to us, we believe him. So "the right," according to this, is the oath.

Some people, in explaining Iblis's mention of the directions of the sons of Adam in His saying: ﴿from before them and from behind them and from their right and from their left﴾ [al-A'raf: 17], went to what we have mentioned about the direction of desires, and said: "What is before them is his deceiving them in what they see; what is behind them is his stealing upon them in secret; from their right is the side of their desires; and from their left is their sight with the heart, and his warning, for the devil may overcome him in it." This applies to those who take them as the specific directions of the son of Adam, and some of them took them as the directions of his affairs and concerns, so the interpretation is broader on this view.

Then God, exalted is He, related the saying of the jinn answering these people: ﴿Rather, you were not believers﴾ as you claimed; rather, you had acquired disbelief and insight into it. We only led you to what we ourselves were led to, and there was no proof or power for us over you except your transgression and your will for disbelief. So the word has come into effect upon all of us, and the punishment has become binding on us, and indeed we are all going to taste it. Tasting here is a metaphor, and it is in this manner that Qatadah and others explained that it is the saying of the jinn up to ﴿astray﴾.

Then God, exalted is He, informed that they all shared in the punishment and were gathered in it, and that this is His treatment of the people of crime, who accumulate sin and disbelief.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 37, verses 35–40:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Indeed, when it was said to them, "There is no deity except Allah," they were arrogant﴾ ﴿and said, "Shall we leave our gods for a mad poet?"﴾ ﴿Rather, he has brought the truth and confirmed the messengers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment,﴾ ﴿and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do,﴾ ﴿except the chosen servants of Allah.﴾

These are the people of sin who were ignorant of Allah, Glorified is He, and who glorified idols and images. So when it was said, "There is no deity except Allah," which is the word of truth and the firmest handhold, arrogance seized them, and it was grievous to them to abandon their idols and the idols of their fathers. Something similar was said concerning Abu Talib, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him, "O uncle, say 'There is no deity except Allah,' a word by which I will testify for you before Allah." Abu Jahl said, "Do you turn away from the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib?" And he said, as his last words, "I am upon the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib." By the Prophet's (ﷺ) presenting to him the saying "There is no deity except Allah," the practice was established of prompting the dying, so that they would oppose the disbelievers and submit to it.

As for the group who said, ﴿Shall we leave our gods for a mad poet?﴾, they were from Quraysh, and their reference to "the mad poet" is to Muhammad (ﷺ). Allah Most High responded to them: that is, the matter is not as they said, that he is a poet; rather, he brought the truth from Allah and confirmed the earlier messengers, such as Moses, Jesus, and Abraham, peace be upon them.

Then Allah Most High informed them, addressing them (and it is permissible that the interpretation be: say to them, O Muhammad): ﴿Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment﴾. Some read "al-'adhāba" in the accusative, and its explanation is that he intended "la-dhā'iqūna," and dropped the nun for lightness; this is a reading that has been deemed erroneous. Abu al-Sammal read [la-dhā'iqun] with tanwin and [al-'adhāba] in the accusative. "Al-alīm" means "al-mu'lim" (the painful).

Then He informed them that this is a recompense for them according to their deeds and what they earned. Then He excepted the servants of Allah with a disconnected exception (istithnā' munqati'), and they are the believers whom Allah Most High has purified for Himself. The majority read "al-mukhlaṣīn" with a fatḥa on the lām, while al-Ḥasan, Qatada, Abu Raja', and Abu 'Amr read it with a kasra on the lām; and this reading found in al-Ṣāffāt has also been transmitted from al-Ḥasan with a fatḥa on the lām.

(p-282) Allah the Exalted says:

﴿Those, for them is a known provision﴾ ﴿fruits, and they are honored﴾ ﴿in Gardens of Bliss﴾ ﴿on couches facing one another﴾ ﴿a cup from a flowing spring is passed around among them﴾ ﴿white, delicious to the drinkers﴾ ﴿in it is no harm (ghawl), nor are they made drunk by it﴾ ﴿and with them are those restrained in glance, with lovely wide eyes﴾ ﴿as if they were a hidden egg﴾.

"Those" (ulā'ika) refers to the sincere servants (of Allah). His saying "known" (ma'lūm) means: it is with them. Their eyes are comforted by knowing the provision that will flow to them, and by knowing that their desires come to them at their appointed times. Otherwise, if that were known only to Allah the Exalted, the people of Paradise would not be singled out for anything. His saying "and they are honored" is an eloquent completion of the bliss, because there is often one who is provided for but not honored, and that is the greatest humiliation.

"Al-surur" is the plural of "sarir" (couch). Abu al-Sammal recited it with a fatha on the first ra'. Concerning this facing one another, there is a narration transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) that they are in the gardens, and the veils are lifted from them so that some of them look at others. Without doubt, some of their times there are spent choosing among their palaces.

"Yutaf" (is passed around) means: the young servants (wildan) go around, as another verse explains. As for "al-ka's" (cup), al-Zajjaj, al-Tabari and others said it is the vessel containing wine or whatever resembles it of drinks (anbidha) and the like. A vessel is called a cup only when this mentioned drink is in it. Al-Dahhak said: every cup in the Qur'an is wine. Some people held that the cup is a specific kind of vessel among vessels: whatever has a wide mouth and no handle. In this they do not consider whether it contains wine or not. His saying "from a flowing spring" (min ma'in) means: from a flowing stream. The mim in ma'in is original (radical), since it is from "the flowing water" (al-ma' al-ma'in). It may also be from "the eye" ('ayn), in which case the mim is an added letter, meaning: from what flows through springs, not hidden, nor kept in a store. The wine of this world is pressed and stored, while the wine of the Hereafter flows in rivers.

His glorified saying "in it" (la fīhā) may refer back to the cup or to the wine, and this is the more apparent. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: the wine of Paradise is whiter than milk. In the recitation (qira'ah) of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it is "yellow" (ṣafrā'). This is described as a quality of the wine alone. "Delicious to the drinkers" means: possessing delight. He described it with a verbal noun (maṣdar) in a broad sense. This usage became so common that it was said "ladhdh" meaning "ladhīdh" (delicious). From this is the saying of the poet:

"By your sweet talk, which if the lions of the wilderness were addressed by it, they would come hastening."

His saying "in it is no ghawl" — "la" is not operative here, because the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) came between it and what it normally governs. Al-ghawl (harm) is a general term for harm. You say: "ghālahu kadhā" when it harmed him secretly. From it comes al-ghīla in killing. The Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning nursing: "I had almost resolved to forbid al-ghīla." From the word is the saying of the poet:

"Our forebears passed away, all of them living in comfort, and the ghūl (calamity) seized me in Makkah."

That is, obstacles blocked me. This is one of the meanings of al-ghawl. From it is the Arab proverb: "What a man he is, how he works!" It is said of a man who is capable and succeeds in every matter he undertakes, or of a man for whom one prays that he accomplish what others have accomplished. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: al-ghawl is a pain in the stomach. Ibn 'Abbas also said, and Qatadah: it is a headache.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The term is more general than all of this. Thus He negated from the wine of Paradise all kinds of harm, since these exist in the wine of this world. Sa'id ibn Jubayr inclined to this generality. From it is the saying of the poet:

"Wine has never ceased to seize us and to take away the first and the foremost."

That is, it harms us by the removal of the intellect.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited "yunzafūna" (they are made drunk) with a fatha on the zay, and likewise in al-Waqi'ah, from your saying: "nazafa al-rajul" when a man became intoxicated, and "nazafathu al-khamr" (the wine intoxicated him). "Al-nazīf" is the intoxicated one. From it is the saying of the poet:

"So I kissed her mouth, seizing its lips, drinking like the intoxicated one drinks cold water of al-Hashraj."

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah interpreted "yunzafūna" as the removal of the intellect. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited it with a kasra on the zay, and likewise in al-Waqi'ah, from "anzafa", with two meanings. One is: he became intoxicated. From it is the saying of Abu al-Ubayrid al-Riyahi:

"By my life, if you became intoxicated or sober, you were a wretched company of drinkers, the family of Abjar."

(p-285) The second is: his drink ran out. It is said: "anzafa al-rajul" when his drink was finished. All of this is negated from the people of Paradise. 'Asim recited it here with a fatha on the zay, and in al-Waqi'ah with a kasra on the zay. Ibn Abi Ishaq recited with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the zay.

His exalted saying: "restrained in glance" (qāṣirāt al-ṭarf). Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Qatadah said: its meaning is: upon their husbands, that is, they do not look at others, and the glance of none of them extends to a stranger. This is the restraint of the glance. "'Īn" is the plural of "'aynā'", who is the one with large eyes in beauty.

As for His exalted saying "as if they were a hidden egg", the people differed as to what is meant. Al-Suddi and Ibn Jubayr said: He likened their colors to the color of the inner membrane of the eggshell, which is the al-ghirqi'. This is the "hidden" (maknūn), that is, protected in a covering. Al-Tabari preferred this, and said: as for the outside of the eggshell, it is not hidden. The majority said: He likened their colors to the color of the shell of an ostrich egg, which is a whiteness mixed with a fine yellowness. They said: the egg itself is mostly hidden by feathers, and whenever a condition occurs in which it is not hidden, it ceases to be an apt comparison. This is the saying of al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Like a young camel of al-Muqanah, whiteness with yellowness, nourished by the flowing water, unmixed."

(p-286) This meaning is abundant in the poetry of the Arabs. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), as transmitted by al-Tabari, said: "al-bayḍ al-maknūn" means by it the protected jewel.

As for "al-ka's" (cup), al-Zajjaj, al-Tabari and others said it is the vessel containing wine or whatever resembles it of drinks (anbidha) and the like. A vessel is called a cup only when this mentioned drink is in it. Al-Dahhak said: every cup in the Qur'an is wine. Some people held that the cup is a specific kind of vessel among vessels: whatever has a wide mouth and no handle. In this they do not consider whether it contains wine or not. His saying "from a flowing spring" (min ma'in) means: from a flowing stream. The mim in ma'in is original (radical), since it is from "the flowing water" (al-ma' al-ma'in). It may also be from "the eye" ('ayn), in which case the mim is an added letter, meaning: from what flows through springs, not hidden, nor kept in a store. The wine of this world is pressed and stored, while the wine of the Hereafter flows in rivers.

His glorified saying "in it" (la fīhā) may refer back to the cup or to the wine, and this is the more apparent. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: the wine of Paradise is whiter than milk. In the recitation (qira'ah) of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it is "yellow" (ṣafrā'). This is described as a quality of the wine alone. "Delicious to the drinkers" means: possessing delight. He described it with a verbal noun (maṣdar) in a broad sense. This usage became so common that it was said "ladhdh" meaning "ladhīdh" (delicious). From this is the saying of the poet:

"By your sweet talk, which if the lions of the wilderness were addressed by it, they would come hastening."

His saying "in it is no ghawl" — "la" is not operative here, because the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) came between it and what it normally governs. Al-ghawl (harm) is a general term for harm. You say: "ghālahu kadhā" when it harmed him secretly. From it comes al-ghīla in killing. The Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning nursing: "I had almost resolved to forbid al-ghīla." From the word is the saying of the poet:

"Our forebears passed away, all of them living in comfort, and the ghūl (calamity) seized me in Makkah."

That is, obstacles blocked me. This is one of the meanings of al-ghawl. From it is the Arab proverb: "What a man he is, how he works!" It is said of a man who is capable and succeeds in every matter he undertakes, or of a man for whom one prays that he accomplish what others have accomplished. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: al-ghawl is a pain in the stomach. Ibn 'Abbas also said, and Qatadah: it is a headache.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The term is more general than all of this. Thus He negated from the wine of Paradise all kinds of harm, since these exist in the wine of this world. Sa'id ibn Jubayr inclined to this generality. From it is the saying of the poet:

"Wine has never ceased to seize us and to take away the first and the foremost."

That is, it harms us by the removal of the intellect.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited "yunzafūna" (they are made drunk) with a fatha on the zay, and likewise in al-Waqi'ah, from your saying: "nazafa al-rajul" when a man became intoxicated, and "nazafathu al-khamr" (the wine intoxicated him). "Al-nazīf" is the intoxicated one. From it is the saying of the poet:

"So I kissed her mouth, seizing its lips, drinking like the intoxicated one drinks cold water of al-Hashraj."

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah interpreted "yunzafūna" as the removal of the intellect. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited it with a kasra on the zay, and likewise in al-Waqi'ah, from "anzafa", with two meanings. One is: he became intoxicated. From it is the saying of Abu al-Ubayrid al-Riyahi:

"By my life, if you became intoxicated or sober, you were a wretched company of drinkers, the family of Abjar."

(p-285) The second is: his drink ran out. It is said: "anzafa al-rajul" when his drink was finished. All of this is negated from the people of Paradise. 'Asim recited it here with a fatha on the zay, and in al-Waqi'ah with a kasra on the zay. Ibn Abi Ishaq recited with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the zay.

His exalted saying: "restrained in glance" (qāṣirāt al-ṭarf). Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Qatadah said: its meaning is: upon their husbands, that is, they do not look at others, and the glance of none of them extends to a stranger. This is the restraint of the glance. "'Īn" is the plural of "'aynā'", who is the one with large eyes in beauty.

As for His exalted saying "as if they were a hidden egg", the people differed as to what is meant. Al-Suddi and Ibn Jubayr said: He likened their colors to the color of the inner membrane of the eggshell, which is the al-ghirqi'. This is the "hidden" (maknūn), that is, protected in a covering. Al-Tabari preferred this, and said: as for the outside of the eggshell, it is not hidden. The majority said: He likened their colors to the color of the shell of an ostrich egg, which is a whiteness mixed with a fine yellowness. They said: the egg itself is mostly hidden by feathers, and whenever a condition occurs in which it is not hidden, it ceases to be an apt comparison. This is the saying of al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Like a young camel of al-Muqanah, whiteness with yellowness, nourished by the flowing water, unmixed."

(p-286) This meaning is abundant in the poetry of the Arabs. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), as transmitted by al-Tabari, said: "al-bayḍ al-maknūn" means by it the protected jewel.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is not authentic in my view from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), because the wording of the verse rejects it.

Another group said: Allah the Exalted likened them to the hidden egg with a general comparison, the whole of the woman to the whole of the egg, and by this He intended the proportion of the parts of the woman: each part's share of excellence relative to its kind is equal to the share of another of its parts relative to its kind. Thus the proportion of her hair to her eye is balanced, since each is a pinnacle in its own kind. The egg is the most proportionate of things in its parts, because from whatever side you approach it, the view of it is one.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 37, verse 50–53:

God, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿So they will turn to one another, questioning each other.﴾ ﴿One of them will say: "I had a companion."﴾ ﴿He used to say: "Are you indeed among those who affirm?"﴾ ﴿"When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be called to account?"﴾

This questioning among the people of Paradise is a questioning of rest and delight. They recall their affairs in Paradise, the affair of the world, and the state of obedience and faith they had in it. Then God, exalted is He, informed us of the words of one of them concerning his own story. He is thus an example for everyone who has a bad companion; this example gives the warning against bad companions and the awareness of their disobedience. He expressed the words of this man in the past tense, since it was a certain matter that had occurred without doubt. Ibn ʿAbbas and others said: these two were from among mankind, a believer and an unbeliever. A group said: they are the two whom God mentioned in His saying: ﴿Woe to me! Would that I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend!﴾ [al-Furqan: 28]. Mujahid said: he was a human and a jinn, one of the disbelieving devils, and the first view is more correct. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "min al-musaddiqin" with a light ṣād, from at-taṣdiq (affirmation). A group read it with a doubled ṣād, from at-taṣaddaq (giving charity).

Furat ibn Thaʿlaba al-Bahrani said in the narrative of these two: they were partners with eight thousand dinars. One of them worshipped God and sought from trade and reflection, while the other was an unbeliever devoted to his wealth. So he dissolved the partnership with the believer, and he remained alone because of the believer's negligence. Then whenever he bought something—a house, a slave-girl, a garden, or the like—he displayed it to that believer and boasted over him. The believer would then go and give in charity an amount similar to that price, in order to buy with it from God in Paradise. So what happened to them in the Hereafter was what this verse contains. Al-Tabari said: this report supports the reading with the doubled ṣād.

"Madinun" means: those who will be recompensed and called to account; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada, and al-Suddi. And ad-din means the recompense, and it has been discussed previously.

The commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 37, verses 54–61:

﴿He said, "Would you like to look?"﴾ ﴿So he looked and saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿He said, "By God, you almost brought me to ruin.﴾ ﴿Had it not been for the favour of my Lord, I would surely have been among those brought forth [to punishment].﴾ ﴿Is it not that we shall not die﴾ ﴿except our first death, and that we shall not be punished?﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is the great triumph.﴾ ﴿For the like of this, let the workers work.﴾

In the speech there is an omitted element, its implied sense being: then some angels present said to this man, "Your companion here is being punished in Hell." He then said at that moment, ﴿Would you like to look?﴾ It is possible that by "you" (antum) he addresses the angels; it is possible that he addresses his companions in Paradise; and it is possible that he addresses his servants. Al-Mahdawi related all of these.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿"muttali'un"﴾ with a fatha on the ṭā' and a shadda. Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of Husayn, read it with a sukun on the ṭā' and a fatha on the nūn. Abu al-Barhasam read it with a sukun on the ṭā' and a kasra on the nūn, taking it as the first-person pronoun. Abu Hatim and others rejected this reading and considered it a grammatical error (laḥḥanūhā), because it combines the ya' of possession (ya' al-idafa) with the nūn of the first person, whereas the correct form would be "muṭli'ī." Abu al-Fath Ibn Jinni defended the reading, saying that he treated the agent (fā'il) as though it were the present-tense verb (nazzala al-fā'il manzilat al-fi'l al-muḍāri'). Al-Tabari cited as evidence the following verse:

"And I do not know—though all my thinking is a thinking—
will he hand me over to my people, Sharahi?"

Al-Farra' said: he means Sharahil.

The majority read ﴿"fa-ṭṭala'a"﴾ with the alif connected (ṣilat al-alif) and the open ṭā' doubled. Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of Husayn, read it with a ḍamma on the alif, a sukun on the ṭā', and a kasra on the lām. This is the reading of Abu al-Barhasam. Al-Zajjaj said: this is the reading of one who reads "muṭli'ūn" with a kasra on the nūn. It is related that the people of Paradise have openings and windows from which they look out over the people of the Fire whenever they wish, by way of retribution and as a lesson, because for them the punishment of the people of the Fire and their rebuke brings joy and comfort. Al-Rummani related this from Abu 'Ali.

"Sawā' al-Jaḥīm" means its middle. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and the people (al-nās) said so. It is called sawā' because the distance from it to its sides is equal. Al-Jaḥīm is the piled-up mass of the fire's embers. It is related from Mutarrif Ibn 'Abd Allah and Khulayd al-'Asri that he saw him, and his appearance (ḥibaruhu wa sibaruhu) had changed, that is, his condition had been transformed; and had God not made him recognise him, he would not have distinguished him. Then the believer said to him at that moment: ﴿By God, you almost brought me to ruin,﴾ that is, you would have destroyed me by your misleading. "Al-radā" means destruction, and from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Did you fear for me destruction on the journey (al-ṭawf)?
And how many a destruction has not spared its people."

In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud the text reads [in kidta latughwīnī], with a waw, from al-ghayy (misguidance). Abu 'Amr al-Dani mentioned it with a rā', from al-ighrā' (enticement). In all of this, the tā' is ḍammed.

﴿Favour of my Lord﴾ is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and this is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of what follows "law-lā" according to Sibawayh. The predicate is omitted, its implied sense being: "it intervened for him" or similar. The meaning of ﴿al-muḥḍarīn﴾ is: in the punishment.

The believer's words: ﴿Is it not that we shall not die﴾ up to his words ﴿nor that we shall be punished?﴾ may be a direct address to his companions in Paradise, when he saw what had befallen his companion and looked at his own condition in Paradise and the condition of his companions, and so he estimated the favour at its true worth. He said to them, by way of questioning, what he said. On this interpretation, the words ﴿Indeed, this is the great triumph﴾ and what follows are connected to his speech, addressed to his companions. It is also possible that ﴿Is it not that we﴾ up to his words [nor that we shall be punished] is an address to his companion by way of rebuke, as if he were saying: where is what you used to say, that we die and there is no punishment or chastisement after death? And the words of God Most High ﴿Indeed, this is the great triumph﴾ up to ﴿let the workers work﴾ may be the believer's address to his companion; this is the view of Qatada. It is also possible that it is God's address to Muhammad ﷺ and his community. This is strengthened by the fact that the believer's words ﴿For the like of this, let the workers work﴾ are said about the Hereafter, which is not a place of work, so it is not appropriate except as a figurative usage. As if he were saying: for the like of this, the workers should have worked.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿"muttali'un"﴾ with a fatha on the ṭā' and a shadda. Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of Husayn, read it with a sukun on the ṭā' and a fatha on the nūn. Abu al-Barhasam read it with a sukun on the ṭā' and a kasra on the nūn, taking it as the first-person pronoun. Abu Hatim and others rejected this reading and considered it a grammatical error (laḥḥanūhā), because it combines the ya' of possession (ya' al-idafa) with the nūn of the first person, whereas the correct form would be "muṭli'ī." Abu al-Fath Ibn Jinni defended the reading, saying that he treated the agent (fā'il) as though it were the present-tense verb (nazzala al-fā'il manzilat al-fi'l al-muḍāri'). Al-Tabari cited as evidence the following verse:

"And I do not know—though all my thinking is a thinking—
will he hand me over to my people, Sharahi?"

Al-Farra' said: he means Sharahil.

The majority read ﴿"fa-ṭṭala'a"﴾ with the alif connected (ṣilat al-alif) and the open ṭā' doubled. Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of Husayn, read it with a ḍamma on the alif, a sukun on the ṭā', and a kasra on the lām. This is the reading of Abu al-Barhasam. Al-Zajjaj said: this is the reading of one who reads "muṭli'ūn" with a kasra on the nūn. It is related that the people of Paradise have openings and windows from which they look out over the people of the Fire whenever they wish, by way of retribution and as a lesson, because for them the punishment of the people of the Fire and their rebuke brings joy and comfort. Al-Rummani related this from Abu 'Ali.

"Sawā' al-Jaḥīm" means its middle. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and the people (al-nās) said so. It is called sawā' because the distance from it to its sides is equal. Al-Jaḥīm is the piled-up mass of the fire's embers. It is related from Mutarrif Ibn 'Abd Allah and Khulayd al-'Asri that he saw him, and his appearance (ḥibaruhu wa sibaruhu) had changed, that is, his condition had been transformed; and had God not made him recognise him, he would not have distinguished him. Then the believer said to him at that moment: ﴿By God, you almost brought me to ruin,﴾ that is, you would have destroyed me by your misleading. "Al-radā" means destruction, and from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Did you fear for me destruction on the journey (al-ṭawf)?
And how many a destruction has not spared its people."

In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud the text reads [in kidta latughwīnī], with a waw, from al-ghayy (misguidance). Abu 'Amr al-Dani mentioned it with a rā', from al-ighrā' (enticement). In all of this, the tā' is ḍammed.

﴿Favour of my Lord﴾ is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and this is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of what follows "law-lā" according to Sibawayh. The predicate is omitted, its implied sense being: "it intervened for him" or similar. The meaning of ﴿al-muḥḍarīn﴾ is: in the punishment.

The believer's words: ﴿Is it not that we shall not die﴾ up to his words ﴿nor that we shall be punished?﴾ may be a direct address to his companions in Paradise, when he saw what had befallen his companion and looked at his own condition in Paradise and the condition of his companions, and so he estimated the favour at its true worth. He said to them, by way of questioning, what he said. On this interpretation, the words ﴿Indeed, this is the great triumph﴾ and what follows are connected to his speech, addressed to his companions. It is also possible that ﴿Is it not that we﴾ up to his words [nor that we shall be punished] is an address to his companion by way of rebuke, as if he were saying: where is what you used to say, that we die and there is no punishment or chastisement after death? And the words of God Most High ﴿Indeed, this is the great triumph﴾ up to ﴿let the workers work﴾ may be the believer's address to his companion; this is the view of Qatada. It is also possible that it is God's address to Muhammad ﷺ and his community. This is strengthened by the fact that the believer's words ﴿For the like of this, let the workers work﴾ are said about the Hereafter, which is not a place of work, so it is not appropriate except as a figurative usage. As if he were saying: for the like of this, the workers should have worked.

(p-٢٩٠) His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying:

﴿Is that better as a hospitality, or the tree of al-Zaqqum?﴾ ﴿Indeed We made it a trial for the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿Indeed it is a tree that springs forth from the root of the Blazing Fire (al-Jahim).﴾ ﴿Its fruit-stalks are like the heads of devils.﴾ ﴿Indeed they will eat from it and fill their bellies with it.﴾ ﴿Then indeed for them upon it is a mixture of boiling water.﴾ ﴿Then indeed their return is to the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿Indeed they found their fathers astray.﴾ ﴿So they are hastened upon their footprints.﴾

The alif in His saying ﴿"Adhalika"﴾ is for taqrir (affirmation through questioning), and the purpose is to make the Quraysh and the disbelievers affirm. The phrase ﴿better as a hospitality﴾ uses the comparative form between two things that share no common ground, since the speech is taqrir, and argumentation requires that the speaker bring his opponent to a choice between two divisions, one of which is corrupt, and lead him by this questioning to choose the other. If the speech were a statement, it would not be permissible, nor would it be beneficial, to say: Paradise is better than the tree of al-Zaqqum. As for His saying ﴿better as a dwelling place﴾ [al-Furqan: 24], it is according to their belief that they have a better dwelling place, and this meaning has already been fully explained.

In some barren regions bordering the deserts there is a bitter, poisonous tree that has a milky sap; if it touches a person's body, it swells and he usually dies from it. It is called the tree of al-Zaqqum. In the speech of the Arabs, tazaqqum means swallowing with great difficulty and effort.

As for His saying ﴿Indeed We made it a trial for the wrongdoers﴾, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Suddi said: it refers to Abu Jahl and his like. That is because, when it was revealed, the disbelievers said: How can Muhammad tell us that the Fire produces trees, when it consumes them and destroys them? Thus they caused themselves and their ignorant followers to be tested by this. Abu Jahl said: al-Zaqqum is only dates with butter, and we eat it as tazaqqum. His saying ﴿in the root of the Blazing Fire﴾ means adjacent to its extremities, which are for it like walls. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: [Indeed it is a tree firmly rooted in the root of the Blazing Fire].

His saying ﴿its fruit-stalks are as if they were the heads of devils﴾: people differed about its meaning. One group said: it is compared to the fruit of a known tree called "the heads of devils," which is in the region of Yemen and is called astan, the one that al-Nabigha mentioned in his saying:

(p-٢٩١) From dark astan trees whose lower parts are black

It is also said that it is the tree called al-sawm, which Sa'idah ibn Ju'ayyah meant in his saying:

Entrusted with the branches of al-sawm, watching over them,
A lean, shrunken-bellied, frail-hearted one from among the pastures.

Another group said: it is compared to the heads of a kind of snake called "devils," which have crests; and from this is the poet's saying:

A thick-maned one, when I swear, you swear,
Like the shaytan of al-himat, most crested.

Another group said: it is compared to what is firmly fixed in souls of the dislike and ugliness of the heads of devils, even though they have not been seen (p-٢٩٢). This is like your saying to one with disheveled, bristling hair and a repulsive appearance: This is the face of a devil. Similar to this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays al-Kindi:

Will he kill me while the sword is my bedfellow,
And blue, sharpened blades like the fangs of ghouls?

He only compared them to what is firmly fixed in souls concerning their form.

Al-shawb means mixing and blending, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. Shayban al-Nahwi read it with a damma on the shin. Al-Zajjaj said: fath (the vowel) on the shin is the verbal noun, and its damma is the noun. Al-hamim means water and the like that is extremely hot. Here it refers to their drink, which is a mud of pus, their discharge, and what flows from them; this is the saying of a group of exegetes.

His saying ﴿then indeed their return﴾ may mean that for them there is a movement of bodies at the time of eating and drinking, then they return to the main part of the Blazing Fire; al-Rummani mentioned this, and it is compared to His saying: ﴿they go around between it and scalding hot water﴾ [al-Rahman: 44]. It may also mean that the return is only from the state of that tormenting eating to the state of burning without eating; and each possibility has been stated. In the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud: [and indeed their overturning is to the Blazing Fire], and in the book of Abu Hatim from him: "maqilahum," from the midday rest.

(p-٢٩٣) His saying ﴿Indeed they found﴾ to the end of the verse is an illustration of the Quraysh. And "yuhra'un": Qatadah, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is: they hasten, as if they are driven with haste. This is their eagerness for disbelief and their greed for it. Al-ihra' is intense travel, Mujahid said, in the manner of a jog in which there is a semblance of trembling; and it is also likely a semblance of the travel of one in terror.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 37, verse 71–79:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿And indeed most of the former peoples went astray before them.﴾ ﴿And indeed We sent among them warners.﴾ ﴿So look, how was the end of those who were warned?﴾ ﴿Except the sincere servants of Allah.﴾ ﴿And Noah had certainly called Us, and how excellent were the Responders.﴾ ﴿And We saved him and his family from the great distress.﴾ ﴿And We made his descendants the survivors.﴾ ﴿And We left for him among the later generations:﴾ ﴿Peace upon Noah among the worlds.﴾

In this verse, the Exalted addresses the Quraysh with the examples of the nations that went astray in earlier times, to whom the warning came, and whom Allah destroyed by His justice. His saying, ﴿So look, how was the end of those who were warned?﴾, requires the report that He punished them, and therefore the exception was fitting in His saying, ﴿Except the servants of Allah.﴾

Noah's call (peace be upon him) included several things: among them, supplication against his people, among them, asking for deliverance, and among them, seeking help. In all of these, the response was given. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and how excellent were the Responders﴾, requires the report that the response was in the most complete form of what Noah (peace be upon him) desired. As for ﴿the great distress﴾, al-Suddi said it is the drowning; and from the distress was the denial of the disbelievers, and riding the water and its terror. Al-Rummani said: the karb (distress) is a heavy news upon the heart.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and Qatadah said: all the people of the earth are from the descendants of Noah. Al-Tabari said: the Arabs are from the sons of Sam, the Sudanese from the sons of Ham, and the Turks, the Saqaliba and others from the sons of Japheth. It was narrated from Samurah ibn Jundub that "the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse and said: 'Sam, Ham and Japheth.'" A group said: Allah, Exalted is He, preserved the descendants of Noah, extended his offspring, and blessed his seed; and the matter is not that the people of the earth were confined to his offspring, rather among the nations are those who do not trace back to him. The first view is better known among the scholars of the Ummah, and they said: Noah is the lesser Adam.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We left for him among the later generations﴾ means: a good and beautiful praise remaining until the end of time, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Suddi. And His saying, ﴿"Peace"﴾ — according to this interpretation — is a nominative beginning, a new sentence, by which Allah greeted him so that mankind might follow that example. Al-Tabari said: this is a security from Him for Noah among the worlds, that anyone should mention him with evil.

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the reward for what he endured patiently for a long time against the statements of the disbelievers and the wicked.

Al-Farra' and others among the Kufans said: His saying, ﴿"Peace"﴾ and the verse that follows, is a clause in the position of accusative after "taraknā" (We left), and this is what is left upon him; as if He said: "And We left upon Noah a greeting by which he is greeted until the Day of Resurrection." In the reading of 'Abdullah: [salāman] in the accusative after "taraknā". May Allah bless Noah and his family and grant them peace, and honour and ennoble them, and (bless) all His prophets.

And ﴿among the later generations﴾ means: among those who remain through the long ages. As for the reading with a kasra on the kha' (al-khākhirīn)... and whatever is of destruction (ihlāk) then it is with a fatha on it.

Al-Tabari said: this is a security from Him for Noah among the worlds, that anyone should mention him with evil.

This is the reward for what he endured patiently for a long time against the statements of the disbelievers and the wicked.

And ﴿among the later generations﴾ means: among those who remain through the long ages. As for the reading with a kasra on the kha' (al-khākhirīn)... and whatever is of destruction (ihlāk) then it is with a fatha on it.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿"Thus" (kadhalika)﴾ refers to His granting Noah what he asked for by way of answering him, and the Exalted praised Noah for his good conduct, for his patience with the harm of his people, his long forbearance toward them, and other aspects of his worship and actions (ﷺ).

There is no explicit text stating that the flood covered all the inhabitants of the earth. However, a group of scholars has said, and has attributed reports, that the flood covered all people except those who were with him in the ark. On this basis arose the view that people today are his descendants. They said: the people at that time were not so numerous, because the era of Adam was recent, and Noah's call and prophethood had reached all of them through the long duration and his remaining among them. So all of them were disbelievers, worshippers of idols, whom the Truth did not attribute to Himself; therefore He drowned all of them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from among his followers (shi'ah)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: the pronoun refers to Noah, peace be upon him, and the meaning is in religion and monotheism. al-Tabari and others related from al-Farra' that the pronoun refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), with the reference being to him. All of this is possible, because "shi'ah" means a common category whose members resemble one another, and "shiya'" means factions. Although the better-known usage is that the one later in time is a follower (shi'ah) of the earlier, there may occur in speech the reverse of this. The poet said:

"And I have none but the family of Ahmad as a shi'ah, and I have none but the path of truth, a path."

So he made them a shi'ah to himself. His saying: ﴿with a sound heart﴾. The commentators said: he means free from doubt and polytheism and all the defects that afflict the hearts of the children of Adam, such as rancour, envy, arrogance and the like. 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: he never cursed anything at all.

It is related that his people had a festival to which they went out, so they invited Ibrahim, peace be upon him, to go out with them. A group said: the meaning of ﴿he glanced a glance at the stars﴾ is: regarding what he perceived concerning the affairs of his people and their condition with them. The majority said: he looked at the stars of the sky.
