﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾ ﴿Then We drowned the others.﴾ ﴿And indeed, among his followers (shi'ah) was Ibrahim,﴾ ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart.﴾ ﴿When he said to his father and his people, "What is it that you worship?"﴾ ﴿Is it a fabrication, gods other than Allah that you desire?﴾ ﴿So what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾ ﴿Then he glanced at the stars,﴾ ﴿and said, "Indeed, I am sick."﴾ ﴿So they turned away from him, retreating.﴾

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿"Thus" (kadhalika)﴾ refers to His granting Noah what he asked for by way of answering him, and the Exalted praised Noah for his good conduct, for his patience with the harm of his people, his long forbearance toward them, and other aspects of his worship and actions (ﷺ).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then We drowned the others﴾ implies that He drowned the people of Noah, his community, and those who denied him. There is no explicit text stating that the flood covered all the inhabitants of the earth. However, a group of scholars has said, and has attributed reports, that the flood covered all people except those who were with him in the ark. On this basis arose the view that people today are his descendants. They said: the people at that time were not so numerous, because the era of Adam was recent, and Noah's call and prophethood had reached all of them through the long duration and his remaining among them. So all of them were disbelievers, worshippers of idols, whom the Truth did not attribute to Himself; therefore He drowned all of them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from among his followers (shi'ah)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: the pronoun refers to Noah, peace be upon him, and the meaning is in religion and monotheism. al-Tabari and others related from al-Farra' that the pronoun refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), with the reference being to him. All of this is possible, because "shi'ah" means a common category whose members resemble one another, and "shiya'" means factions. Although the better-known usage is that the one later in time is a follower (shi'ah) of the earlier, there may occur in speech the reverse of this. The poet said:

"And I have none but the family of Ahmad as a shi'ah, and I have none but the path of truth, a path."

So he made them a shi'ah to himself. His saying: ﴿with a sound heart﴾. The commentators said: he means free from doubt and polytheism and all the defects that afflict the hearts of the children of Adam, such as rancour, envy, arrogance and the like. 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: he never cursed anything at all.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is it a fabrication, gods other than Allah that you desire?﴾ "A'ifkan" is an interrogative with the meaning of affirmation, i.e., "Is it falsehood and nonsense, gods other than Allah that you desire?" "Alihah" is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "ifkan", and the original hamzah of "ifk" was eased. ﴿So what is your opinion﴾ is rebuke, warning and threat.

Then the Exalted reported about Ibrahim's glance at the stars, peace be upon him. It is related that his people had a festival to which they went out, so they invited Ibrahim, peace be upon him, to go out with them. He then looked and excused himself on account of sickness, intending to remain behind, contrary to them, to the idols. Ibn Zayd, from his father, said: their king sent to him that tomorrow is a festival, so attend with us. He looked at a rising star and said: "Indeed, this rises along with my sickness." A group said: the meaning of ﴿he glanced a glance at the stars﴾ is: regarding what he perceived concerning the affairs of his people and their condition with them. The majority said: he looked at the stars of the sky. It is related that the science of the stars was among them, studied and in use, so he deceived them through that direction, because they were people of herding and agriculture, and these two livelihoods require looking at the stars.

Regarding his saying ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾, there is disagreement. A group said: it is a lie concerning God's sake; he informed them about himself that he was ill, and that the planet had given him that. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: he pointed for them to an illness and sickness that is contagious, like the plague, and for this reason they turned away retreating, that is, fleeing from him. Others said: rather, they turned away retreating because of their disbelief and their contempt for his matter. On this interpretation, that it was a lie, the hadith comes: "Ibrahim did not lie except three lies: his saying, 'Indeed, I am sick'; his saying, 'Rather, this, their chief, did it'; and his saying concerning Sarah, 'She is my sister'."

Another group said: it is not a lie, and lying is not permissible for him; rather it is an allusion (ma'arid), he informed them that he was sick in property, and according to the custom of the children of Adam, since a child of Adam must inevitably fall sick by necessity. It was said on this basis: he meant, "I am sick in soul because of your affairs and your disbelief," so it appeared to them from his speech that he meant bodily sickness present; and such are allusions. This interpretation is not refuted by the hadith and its mention of the lies, because it may be said of them that they are lies in an extended sense according to the belief of the one who speaks. The lie that is the intention of uttering falsehood and informing contrary to what is in the soul, without a legitimate benefit, is the one that is not permissible for the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 37, verses 91–98:**

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿Then he turned to their gods and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ ﴿"What is wrong with you that you do not speak?"﴾ ﴿Then he turned upon them, striking with the right hand.﴾ ﴿Then they came hastening toward him.﴾ ﴿He said, "Do you worship what you carve?"﴾ ﴿"And Allah created you and what you do."﴾ ﴿They said, "Build for him a structure and throw him into the blaze."﴾ ﴿So they intended a plot against him, but We made them the lowest.﴾

"Rāgha" (راغَ) means "he inclined," and from it comes the verse of 'Adī ibn Zayd:

*"Where turning aside (al-riyāgh) benefits not, nor does [anything] benefit, except the sincere, skilled one."*

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Will you not eat?﴾ is said in mockery of the worshippers of those idols. It is narrated that the custom of those people was to leave food in the houses of the idols, believing that the idols would take some of its scent, and similar false beliefs. Then the servants of the house would eat it. When Ibrahim, peace be upon him, entered, he stood over the food, addressing the idols and speaking to them, and his purpose was to mock their worshippers. Then he turned at that moment to striking those idols with an axe until he reduced them to fragments.

Scholars differed about the meaning of His saying ﴿"with the right hand"﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "with his right hand." It was also said that it means "with his strength," because he gathered both his hands on the axe. It was also said that it refers to the oath of swearing in His saying ﴿"And by Allah, I will surely plan against your idols"﴾ [al-Anbiya: 57]. The word "ḍarban" (ضَرْبًا) is in the accusative as an infinitive (maṣdar) governed by an implied verb of the same root. In the codex of 'Abdullah, the reading is [ṣafqan bil-yamīn].

The pronoun in His saying "aqbalū" (أقْبَلُوا) refers to the disbelievers of his people. The majority read ﴿"yaziffūn"﴾ with a fatha on the yā', from zaffa, meaning "he hastened," and zaffat al-ibil (زَفَّتِ الإبِلُ) means "the camels hastened." From it is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

*"The leader of the young camels came before their weaning, hastening, and the [she-camels] came behind him, quickly."*

From it is also the verse of the Hudhalī:

*"And the young camels hastened in the cold of evening, as the ostriches hasten to their nest, the spirited one."*

Ḥamza alone read ﴿"yuziffūn"﴾ with a ḍamma on the yā', from azaffa, meaning "he entered into zafīf (the rapid gait)." It is not a causative form of transitivity. This is one view. Abū 'Alī said its meaning is: "they carry others to hasten." He related this from al-Aṣmaʿī, and it is the reading of Mujāhid, Ibn Wathhāb, and al-A'mash. Mujāhid and 'Abdullah ibn Zayd read ﴿"yazifūn"﴾ with a fatha on the yā' and a light fā', from wazafa, yazifu, but this is a rejected dialect. Al-Kisā'ī and al-Farrā' said: "We do not recognize it with the meaning of zaffa." Mujāhid said: "al-wazīf" means "flowing."

A group went to the view that ﴿"yazifūn"﴾ means that they walk slowly in their steps like the gait of a bride. The meaning is that they were confident that no one could harm their gods, because of their might, so they were therefore unhurried. However, zaffa in the sense of "hastened" is the well-known meaning.

Then Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said to them, within a lengthy dialogue that the verse contains: ﴿"Do you worship what you carve?"﴾, that is: Do you make a god, to be venerated, out of something you have made from wood or stone and fashioned with your own hands? He informed them of a fact that they could not deny, which is His saying ﴿"And Allah created you"﴾. The commentators differed about His saying ﴿"and what you do"﴾. The view of a group of exegetes (tafsir) is that "mā" (ما) is verbal-masdariyya (infinitival), and the meaning is "and your actions." This verse, according to them, is a principle concerning the creation of human acts, and this agrees with the position of Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna, i.e., Sunni orthodoxy) on this matter. Another group said it is in the sense of "alladhī" (the one which). Another group said "mā" is interrogative, and another said it is negative, meaning: "and you do not do anything at the time of your creation nor before it, and you have no power over anything." The Mu'tazila are compelled to depart from making "mā" a masdariyya.

As for "al-bunyān" (البُنْيانُ), it was said that it was at the location where the fire was kindled. It was also said that it was rather for the catapult from which he was thrown. The account of Ibrahim's fire has already been mentioned earlier. Allah made them "the lowest" by their being defeated, humiliated, and overtaken by punishments.

His, the Exalted and Majestic's, saying:

﴿He said: "Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me." "My Lord, grant me [a son] from among the righteous." So We gave him the good tidings of a forbearing boy. And when he reached with him the age of exertion, he said: "O my son, indeed I have seen in a dream that I am slaughtering you, so see what you think." He said: "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast."﴾

A group said: Ibrahim's saying ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord﴾ was after his emergence from the Fire, and that by his going he indicated his emigration from the land of Babylon, where the kingdom of Nimrod was, so he went out to al-Sham. It is narrated that he went to the lands of Egypt. Another group said: his saying ﴿Indeed I am going﴾ does not mean emigration, as in another verse, but rather that he meant meeting Allah after being burned. However, he thought that he would die in the Fire, so he said this statement before he was cast into the Fire. It is as if he said: "I am proceeding by this deed to my Lord, and He will guide me to Paradise." Qatadah inclined to this meaning. For those who know this going, there is attachment and argument regarding purity [of the heart]. It is a good interpretation of ﴿Indeed I am going﴾ on its own. The first view is more apparent in light of the context of the verse that follows it, because guidance is connected to it, and so is the supplication regarding the child. This does not hold with the going of annihilation.

As for his saying ﴿from among the righteous﴾: the word "min" (from) is partitive, meaning: a child who will be counted among the righteous.

As for his saying ﴿So We gave him the good tidings﴾: many scholars, among them al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, who traced it to the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ali, and Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Mas'ud, and Ka'b, and Ubayd ibn Umayr, said: it is the well-known good tidings of Ishaq, and he is the one who was to be sacrificed. The command to sacrifice him was in al-Sham. Ata and Muqatil said: it was in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Some others said: rather it was in the Hijaz, where he came with his father on the Buraq (a legendary steed). Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the good tidings mentioned after this in this verse is the good tidings of his prophethood, as Allah the Exalted said about Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿And We gave him, out of Our mercy, his brother Harun as a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 53]. He had already been given him before that, but what was meant was prophethood, so likewise here. This group said, regarding the Bedouin's saying "O son of the two sacrificed ones": he meant Ishaq, and the paternal uncle is called a father. It was also said: he was commanded to sacrifice him after Ya'qub had been born to him, so the command to sacrifice did not conflict with the good tidings of his son and his son's son.

Another group said: this good tidings was regarding Isma'il, peace be upon him, and he is the one who was to be sacrificed. The command to sacrifice him was in the Hijaz and Mina, and Muhammad (ﷺ) [...] then Ibrahim, peace be upon him, stoned the Shaytan with pebbles, took the ram, and established the rites. This is also the view of Ibn Abbas and Ibn Amr, may Allah be pleased with them both. It is narrated from al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan (Mu'awiyah traced it to the Prophet (ﷺ)), and Muhammad ibn Ka'b. My father, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say this, and he would argue from the Bedouin's saying to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O son of the two sacrificed ones," and from his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "I am the son of the two sacrificed ones," meaning Isma'il and his father Abdullah. He would also argue that the good tidings were coupled with the statement that after him would come Ya'qub. So if it had been said to him in his childhood, "Sacrifice him," that would have contradicted the good tidings of Ya'qub, peace be upon him. He would also argue from the apparent meaning of this verse that he was given the good tidings of Isma'il, and the matter of his sacrifice ended, then after that he was given the good tidings of Ishaq. I heard him say: Ibrahim would come from al-Sham to Makkah on the Buraq, visiting, and return the same day. This has been mentioned by al-Tha'labi from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, but he did not mention that this was on the Buraq. He mentioned the story from Ibn Ishaq, and in it there is mention of the Buraq, as I heard my father relate.

al-Tabari mentioned that Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the one sacrificed is Isma'il, and the Jews claim it is Ishaq, but the Jews lied. He also mentioned that Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, may Allah be pleased with him, asked a Jewish man who had become Muslim and whose Islam was good, and he said: the one sacrificed is Isma'il, peace be upon him, and the Jews know this, but they envy you, O Arab people, that this verse and this virtue, by Allah, should be for your father.

As for "al-sa'y" (the exertion) in this verse: it means work, worship, and assistance. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd. Qatadah said: al-sa'y is walking on foot, meaning a firm striving. This is similar in meaning to the first view. al-Dahhak recited: "ma'ahu al-sa'ya wa asarra fi nafsihi huznan" (with him the striving, and he concealed in himself grief), and he said: this is also how it is in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, and it is the recitation of al-A'mash. As for his saying ﴿Indeed I have seen in a dream that I am slaughtering you﴾: it may be that he saw this with his own eyes, and the dreams of the prophets are revelation, and the time for carrying it out was specified for him. It may also be that he was commanded in his sleep to sacrifice him, and he expressed that, meaning: "Indeed I saw in sleep what requires that I sacrifice you."

Most people recited ﴿"Maza tara"﴾ (what do you see) with a fatha on the ta' and the ra'. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited "Maza turi" (what do you show) with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ra', meaning: what appears from you of endurance or distress. This is the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, al-Aswad ibn Yazid, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, al-A'mash, and Mujahid. al-A'mash and al-Dahhak recited with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the ra', in the passive verb form. As for the first, it is from the sight of opinion (ru'yat al-ra'y), a verb that transitively takes one object, which in this verse is either "maza" (taking the two together as one noun), or "dha" (taking it to mean "alladhi", with "ma" being interrogative, and the pronoun omitted from the relative clause). As for the second recitation, the grammatical object is as already explained in the first, except that the verb here is transferred from: "Zayd saw the thing" and "I showed him it," but it is of the pattern of "a'taytu" (I gave), so it is permissible to limit it to one of the two objects. As for the second recitation, Abu Ali criticized it, and it can be justified with some strain. In the mushaf (codex) of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads: [do what you are commanded].

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (*al-Muharrar al-Wajiz*) on Surah 37, verses 103–111:**

The Exalted said:

﴿So when they both had submitted, and he put him down upon his forehead,﴾ ﴿We called out to him, "O Abraham,﴾ ﴿you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this was a clear trial.﴾ ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾ ﴿And We left for him among later generations:﴾ ﴿"Peace upon Abraham."﴾ ﴿Thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾

Most of the reciters read ﴿"أسْلَما" (aslamā)﴾, meaning they surrendered themselves (*anfusahuma*) and submitted to Allah. 'Ali, 'Abdullah, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Thawri read ﴿"سَلَّما" (sallamā)﴾, meaning they entrusted the matter to Him in His decree and His destiny, and submitted to His command. So Abraham submitted his son, and the son submitted himself.

The grammarians differed over the response (*jawab*) of ﴿"لَمّا" (lammā)﴾. The Kufans said the response is ﴿"نادَيْناهُ" (nādaynāhu)﴾, and the waw is extra. One group said the response is ﴿"تَلَّهُ" (tallahu)﴾, and the waw is extra, like its extra use in ﴿"وَفُتِحَتِ السَماءُ" (wa-futiḥat al-samā')﴾ [al-Naba' 19]. The Basrans said the response is omitted, its estimated form being: "When they both had submitted, they both submitted, and he put him down." This is the view of Sibawayh and al-Khalil, and according to them it is like the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*"So when we crossed the courtyard of the tribe, and it veered with us toward the belly of a sandy valley with winding dunes,"*

the estimate being: "When we crossed the courtyard of the tribe, we crossed, and it veered." Some Basrans said the response is omitted, its estimated form being: "When they both had submitted and he put him down upon his forehead, his reward was made abundant," or something similar to this, as the meaning requires.

The words of the Exalted ﴿"وَتَلَّهُ" (wa-tallahu)﴾ mean: he placed him down with force. From this is the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) put him down (*fatallahu*) in his hand," meaning he placed him with force. The word *tall* (a mound of earth) is derived from this, as if it was placed down at that spot. The words ﴿"لِلْجَبِينِ" (lil-jabīn)﴾ mean: toward that side and upon it, as in the proverb they say: "for the two hands and the mouth," and as you say: "he fell onto his left side." Sa'ida ibn Juwayya said:

*"So he lay prostrate upon the two foreheads."*

The two *jabīnayn* are the two sides of the forehead, one here and one there.

It is narrated in the stories about this verse that the one being sacrificed said to his father: "Tighten my bonds with the rope, lest I thrash about. Turn your gaze away from me, lest you feel mercy for me, and turn my face toward the ground." Qatada said: "He turned him onto his face and took the knife." The phrase ﴿"وَتَلَّهُ لِلْجَبِينِ"﴾ does not require that the face be toward the ground; rather it describes the position of one slaughtered on his side, facing the *qibla*.

The words ﴿"أنْ يا إبْراهِيمُ" (an yā Ibrāhīm)﴾ are explanatory (*mufassira*), and have no place in the grammatical structure (*i'rab*, the grammatical inflection of words in a sentence).

The words of the Exalted ﴿"قَدْ صَدَّقْتَ الرُؤْيا" (qad ṣaddaqta al-ru'yā)﴾ may mean: "with your heart," in the sense that your vision was true and a truth from Allah. So you acted in accordance with it when you believed in it and held its truth to be certain. It may also mean: you confirmed through your action what had arisen from the vision within yourself, as if He said: "You have fulfilled its due from action." The word *ru'yā* (vision) is the name for what is seen from Allah in sleep, while *ḥulm* (dream) is the name for what is seen from Satan. From this is the authentic hadith: "The vision is from Allah, and the dream is from Satan."

The words of the Exalted ﴿"إنّا كَذَلِكَ" (innā kadhālika)﴾ refer to what Abraham did. It is as if He said: "Indeed, with this kind of sincerity and obedience, We reward the doers of good." The words ﴿"إنَّ هَذا" (inna hādhā)﴾ may refer to the trial and test by hardship contained in the story, and may also refer to the joy of the ransom and the deliverance from that hardship when the slaughter was to be carried out, in which case *al-balā'* (the trial) carries the meaning of a blessing. A group of the exegetes pointed to each of these possibilities. In a hadith: "Allah the Exalted revealed to Isaac: 'Indeed, because of your patience with My command, I have granted you a supplication, in which I will give you whatever you ask, so ask Me.' He said: 'O Lord, any servant who meets You from among the first and the last, not associating anything with You, admit him to Paradise.'"

The pronoun in ﴿"فَدَيْناهُ" (fadaynāhu)﴾ refers to the slaughter, and *dhibḥ* (the slaughter) is the name for what is slaughtered. He described it as great because it was certainly accepted. This was said by Mujahid. 'Umar ibn 'Ubayd said: *dhibḥ* is the ram, and it is great because the Sunna was established by it and because it became a religious practice that remains until the end of time. al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: it was great because it came from Allah. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: it was great because it did not come from offspring but from creation. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that its greatness lies in its being one of the rams of Paradise, which grazed there for forty autumns. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the ram which the son of Adam offered as a sacrifice. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: it was a mountain goat (*wa'l*) sent down upon him from Thabir. The majority said: it was a white ram, with curled horns and wide eyes, which he found behind him tied to an acacia tree. It is narrated that it broke loose, and he pursued it and threw pebbles at it at the places of the *jamarat* (the stoning pillars), and by that the Sunna was established. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: he stoned Satan at the Jamrat al-'Aqaba and at the others. This has already been mentioned.

The people of the Sunna (*Ahl al-Sunna*, the mainstream Sunni tradition) hold that in this story the resolve to act was abrogated (*nusikha*, i.e., nullified by later revelation), while the Mu'tazila (*al-Mu'tazila*, a theological school) say that abrogation is not valid except after the act has actually occurred. The exegetes split over this verse into two groups. One group said: the slaughter took place and was completed after that. This is plainly a lie. Another group from among them said: rather, Abraham had seen in his dream only the drawing of the blade across the throat, so he thought it was a slaughter, prepared for it, and carried it out. When what he had seen came to pass, the abrogation occurred.

The Basrans said the response is omitted, its estimated form being: "When they both had submitted, they both submitted, and he put him down." This is the view of Sibawayh and al-Khalil, and according to them it is like the words of Imru' al-Qays:

the estimate being: "When we crossed the courtyard of the tribe, we crossed, and it veered." Some Basrans said the response is omitted, its estimated form being: "When they both had submitted and he put him down upon his forehead, his reward was made abundant," or something similar to this, as the meaning requires.

From this is the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) put him down (*fatallahu*) in his hand," meaning he placed him with force. The word *tall* (a mound of earth) is derived from this, as if it was placed down at that spot. The words ﴿"لِلْجَبِينِ" (lil-jabīn)﴾ mean: toward that side and upon it, as in the proverb they say: "for the two hands and the mouth," and as you say: "he fell onto his left side." Sa'ida ibn Juwayya said:

The two *jabīnayn* are the two sides of the forehead, one here and one there.

It is narrated in the stories about this verse that the one being sacrificed said to his father: "Tighten my bonds with the rope, lest I thrash about. Turn your gaze away from me, lest you feel mercy for me, and turn my face toward the ground." Qatada said: "He turned him onto his face and took the knife." The phrase ﴿"وَتَلَّهُ لِلْجَبِينِ"﴾ does not require that the face be toward the ground; rather it describes the position of one slaughtered on his side, facing the *qibla*.

So you acted in accordance with it when you believed in it and held its truth to be certain. It may also mean: you confirmed through your action what had arisen from the vision within yourself, as if He said: "You have fulfilled its due from action." The word *ru'yā* (vision) is the name for what is seen from Allah in sleep, while *ḥulm* (dream) is the name for what is seen from Satan. From this is the authentic hadith: "The vision is from Allah, and the dream is from Satan."

When what he had seen came to pass, the abrogation occurred.

There is no disagreement that Abraham drew the blade across his son's throat, but it did not cut.

It is narrated that a sheet of copper came between them with its edge, and Allah knows best how it was. Most of the reciters read ﴿"أسْلَما" (aslamā)﴾, meaning they surrendered themselves (*anfusahuma*) and submitted to Allah. 'Ali, 'Abdullah, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Thawri read ﴿"سَلَّما" (sallamā)﴾, meaning they entrusted the matter to Him in His decree and His destiny, and submitted to His command. So Abraham submitted his son, and the son submitted himself.

The grammarians differed over the response (*jawab*) of ﴿"لَمّا" (lammā)﴾. The Kufans said the response is ﴿"نادَيْناهُ" (nādaynāhu)﴾, and the waw is extra. One group said the response is ﴿"تَلَّهُ" (tallahu)﴾, and the waw is extra, like its extra use in ﴿"وَفُتِحَتِ السَماءُ" (wa-futiḥat al-samā')﴾ [al-Naba' 19]. The Basrans said the response is omitted, its estimated form being: "When they both had submitted, they both submitted, and he put him down." This is the view of Sibawayh and al-Khalil, and according to them it is like the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*"So when we crossed the courtyard of the tribe, and it veered with us toward the belly of a sandy valley with winding dunes,"*

the estimate being: "When we crossed the courtyard of the tribe, we crossed, and it veered." Some Basrans said the response is omitted, its estimated form being: "When they both had submitted and he put him down upon his forehead, his reward was made abundant," or something similar to this, as the meaning requires.

The words of the Exalted ﴿"وَتَلَّهُ" (wa-tallahu)﴾ mean: he placed him down with force. From this is the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) put him down (*fatallahu*) in his hand," meaning he placed him with force. The word *tall* (a mound of earth) is derived from this, as if it was placed down at that spot. The words ﴿"لِلْجَبِينِ" (lil-jabīn)﴾ mean: toward that side and upon it, as in the proverb they say: "for the two hands and the mouth," and as you say: "he fell onto his left side." Sa'ida ibn Juwayya said:

*"So he lay prostrate upon the two foreheads."*

The two *jabīnayn* are the two sides of the forehead, one here and one there.

It is narrated in the stories about this verse that the one being sacrificed said to his father: "Tighten my bonds with the rope, lest I thrash about. Turn your gaze away from me, lest you feel mercy for me, and turn my face toward the ground." Qatada said: "He turned him onto his face and took the knife." The phrase ﴿"وَتَلَّهُ لِلْجَبِينِ"﴾ does not require that the face be toward the ground; rather it describes the position of one slaughtered on his side, facing the *qibla*.

The words ﴿"أنْ يا إبْراهِيمُ" (an yā Ibrāhīm)﴾ are explanatory (*mufassira*), and have no place in the grammatical structure (*i'rab*, the grammatical inflection of words in a sentence).

The words of the Exalted ﴿"قَدْ صَدَّقْتَ الرُؤْيا" (qad ṣaddaqta al-ru'yā)﴾ may mean: "with your heart," in the sense that your vision was true and a truth from Allah. So you acted in accordance with it when you believed in it and held its truth to be certain. It may also mean: you confirmed through your action what had arisen from the vision within yourself, as if He said: "You have fulfilled its due from action." The word *ru'yā* (vision) is the name for what is seen from Allah in sleep, while *ḥulm* (dream) is the name for what is seen from Satan. From this is the authentic hadith: "The vision is from Allah, and the dream is from Satan."

The words of the Exalted ﴿"إنّا كَذَلِكَ" (innā kadhālika)﴾ refer to what Abraham did. It is as if He said: "Indeed, with this kind of sincerity and obedience, We reward the doers of good." The words ﴿"إنَّ هَذا" (inna hādhā)﴾ may refer to the trial and test by hardship contained in the story, and may also refer to the joy of the ransom and the deliverance from that hardship when the slaughter was to be carried out, in which case *al-balā'* (the trial) carries the meaning of a blessing. A group of the exegetes pointed to each of these possibilities. In a hadith: "Allah the Exalted revealed to Isaac: 'Indeed, because of your patience with My command, I have granted you a supplication, in which I will give you whatever you ask, so ask Me.' He said: 'O Lord, any servant who meets You from among the first and the last, not associating anything with You, admit him to Paradise.'"

The pronoun in ﴿"فَدَيْناهُ" (fadaynāhu)﴾ refers to the slaughter, and *dhibḥ* (the slaughter) is the name for what is slaughtered. He described it as great because it was certainly accepted. This was said by Mujahid. 'Umar ibn 'Ubayd said: *dhibḥ* is the ram, and it is great because the Sunna was established by it and because it became a religious practice that remains until the end of time. al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: it was great because it came from Allah. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: it was great because it did not come from offspring but from creation. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that its greatness lies in its being one of the rams of Paradise, which grazed there for forty autumns. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the ram which the son of Adam offered as a sacrifice. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: it was a mountain goat (*wa'l*) sent down upon him from Thabir. The majority said: it was a white ram, with curled horns and wide eyes, which he found behind him tied to an acacia tree. It is narrated that it broke loose, and he pursued it and threw pebbles at it at the places of the *jamarat* (the stoning pillars), and by that the Sunna was established. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: he stoned Satan at the Jamrat al-'Aqaba and at the others. This has already been mentioned.

The people of the Sunna (*Ahl al-Sunna*, the mainstream Sunni tradition) hold that in this story the resolve to act was abrogated (*nusikha*, i.e., nullified by later revelation), while the Mu'tazila (*al-Mu'tazila*, a theological school) say that abrogation is not valid except after the act has actually occurred. The exegetes split over this verse into two groups. One group said: the slaughter took place and was completed after that. This is plainly a lie. Another group from among them said: rather, Abraham had seen in his dream only the drawing of the blade across the throat, so he thought it was a slaughter, prepared for it, and carried it out. When what he had seen came to pass, the abrogation occurred.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no disagreement that Abraham drew the blade across his son's throat, but it did not cut.

It is narrated that a sheet of copper came between them with its edge, and Allah knows best how it was. The people have multiplied the stories about this verse with material whose authenticity is non-existent, so I have abbreviated it. The interpretation of similar wording has already been given: ﴿"وَتَرَكْنا عَلَيْهِ في الآخِرِينَ" (wa-taraknā 'alayhi fi'l-ākhirīn)﴾ and ﴿"سَلامٌ عَلى إبْراهِيمَ" (salāmun 'alā Ibrāhīm)﴾. The words of the Exalted ﴿"كَذَلِكَ نَجْزِي المُحْسِنِينَ" (kadhālika najzī al-muḥsinīn)﴾ mean: by the like of this action. The rest of the verse is clear.

Among the things that are considered strange about this verse is that 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: it was slaughtered at the Maqam (the Station of Abraham). Al-Tabari reported from a group whom he did not name that they said: the command, the sharpening of the knife and the whole story took place in Syria. The majority said: it was slaughtered at Mina. al-Sha'bi said: "I saw the two horns of Abraham's ram hanging in the Ka'ba."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 37, verses 112–117:

His the Exalted and Majestic's saying:

﴿And We gave him the glad tidings of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are the good-doer and the one who clearly wrongs himself.﴾ ﴿And We certainly bestowed favour upon Moses and Aaron.﴾ ﴿And We delivered them and their people from the great distress.﴾ ﴿And We helped them, so they were the victorious.﴾ ﴿And We gave them the clear Book.﴾

Whoever says that the one who was sacrificed was Ishmael makes this glad tidings the glad tidings of Isaac's birth, which is the glad tidings repeated in more than one surah. Whoever makes the one sacrificed Isaac makes this glad tidings only for prophethood itself.

The favour upon Moses and Aaron lies in prophethood and all that accompanied it of their standing with Allah. "The great distress" is the enslavement of the Copts over them, then Pharaoh's army when the Children of Israel said, "Indeed, we are overtaken" (Q. 26:61), then the sea after that. The pronoun in "We helped them" refers to the group mentioned earlier, namely Moses, Aaron and their people. Some said: it means Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them, but the pronoun was expressed in the plural form as a mark of honour; this is among the things the Arabs do, referring to the one they revere with a plural expression. "The clear Book" is the Torah.

And concerning His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿And We guided them both to the straight path.﴾ ﴿And We left for them [a good name] among the later generations.﴾ ﴿Peace be upon Moses and Aaron.﴾ ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, they were two of Our believing servants.﴾ ﴿And indeed, Elias was among the messengers.﴾ ﴿When he said to his people, "Will you not be mindful of God?"﴾ ﴿Do you call upon Baal and forsake the best of creators?﴾

﴿The straight path﴾: by it He means in this verse the path of the Law (shar') and of prophethood (nubuwwah) that leads to God, Exalted is He. The discussion of a similar phrase has already preceded, in His saying: ﴿And We left for them [a good name] among the later generations﴾ ﴿Peace be upon Moses and Aaron.﴾

Ilyas (Elias) is one of the prophets of God, Exalted is He. Qatada and Ibn Mas'ud said: he is Idris, peace be upon him. al-Tabari said: he is Ilyas ibn Yasin, ibn Finhas, ibn al-'Ayzar, ibn Harun, ibn 'Imran. A group said: he is a descendant of Aaron, peace be upon him.

The majority of reciters read ﴿"wa-inna Ilyas"﴾ with a kasra on the hamzah, and it is a proper noun. Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Muhaysin, 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan, and al-A'raj read "wa-inna al-Yas" without hamzah and with the alif pronounced as a connecting vowel. This may be justified in one of two ways. Either the hamzah has been dropped, as Ibn Kathir dropped it in his saying: [Indeed, it is one of the greatest (calamities)], meaning: li-iḥdā (the "la" plus "iḥdā"), so that the separate word is treated as if it were joined, as is often done in many matters. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 37, verse 126–138:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Allah, your Lord and the Lord of your earliest forefathers.﴾ ﴿But they denied him, so they will surely be brought forth.﴾ ﴿Except the sincere servants of Allah.﴾ ﴿And We left for him among the later generations:﴾ ﴿Peace be upon the family of Yasin.﴾ ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾ ﴿And indeed, Lot was among the messengers.﴾ ﴿When We saved him and his family, all of them,﴾ ﴿except an old woman among those who remained behind.﴾ ﴿Then We destroyed the others.﴾ ﴿And indeed, you pass by them in the morning,﴾ ﴿and at night. Will you not then use your reason?﴾

(p-309) Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read all of them (al-jami') in the accusative (nasb), as a substitution (badal) for His saying: "ahsana" (the verb "ahsana" in the preceding verse), while the rest of the readers, and 'Asim also, read them in the nominative (raf'), as a fresh sentence (qat' wa-al-istl'naf, i.e., a new, independent clause). The pronoun in "kadhdhabuhu" (they denied him) refers to the people of Ilyas (Elias). And "muhdarun" (brought forth) means: gathered for the punishment of Allah. The explanation of the rest of the verse has already been given, as has the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Peace be upon the family of Yasin.﴾

As for Lot: it is said he was the son of his sister. His story has been mentioned in full already. His wife was the old woman who was destroyed, and she was a disbeliever. Either she was concealing her disbelief from him, or she openly displayed it. Marrying idolatresses and remaining married to them was permissible. "Al-ghabirun" (those who remain behind) means those who are left: the verb "ghabara" means "baqiya" (remained), and its meaning here is: she remained among those who were destroyed.

Then, exalted is He, addressed the Quraysh, or it is in the sense of: say to them, O Muhammad: "And indeed, you pass by them in the morning and at night. It is necessary that you take heed and reflect." Then He rebuked them with His saying: ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾

The Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 37, verses 139–146:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And indeed, Yunus was among the messengers.﴾ ﴿When he fled to the laden ship.﴾ ﴿Then he drew lots, and was among the losers.﴾ ﴿Then the fish swallowed him, and he was blameworthy.﴾ ﴿So had he not been of those who glorify Allah.﴾ ﴿He would have remained in its belly until the day they are resurrected.﴾ ﴿Then We cast him onto the open land while he was ailing.﴾ ﴿And We caused a gourd-plant to grow over him.﴾

He is Yunus ibn Matta, peace be upon him, from the Children of Israel. It is narrated that he was made a prophet at the age of twenty-eight, and he buckled under the burdens of prophethood as a rope-bridge (or a weak vessel) buckles under a load. His story has already been explained, but we will mention from it what is needed to understand these words.

It is narrated that Allah sent him to his people. He called them once, and they opposed him, so he threatened them with punishment. Allah informed him of its day, and Yunus set that time for them. Then, when his people saw the signs of the punishment before it reached them, they repented and believed, so Allah accepted their repentance and turned the punishment away from them. This was a test for Yunus, peace be upon him, and anger overtook Yunus. It is also related that it was among their custom that they would kill the liar if no clear proof was established for him. Yunus feared them, and in addition he was angry, so he fled to the ship. That is, he intended to escape and entered the sea. He expressed his escape with the word *ibaq* (running away from one's master), since he was a servant of Allah who fled without the permission of his master; this is the literal meaning of *ibaq*. "Al-Fulk" in this context is singular, and "al-mashhun" means the loaded (heavy-laden). (p-310) Here there is a narrative that has been omitted for brevity and conciseness.

It is related from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that when he was in the ship, it moved away and nearly sank and did not go on, while the other ships were moving to the right and left. The people of the ship said: "Among us there is one with a sin, and because of him Allah is holding us back." They said: "Let us draw lots." So they took for each person a lot, and said: "O Allah, let the lot of the sinner float, and let the lots of others sink." So the lot of Yunus floated. They did this three times, and each time the lot fell on him. They resolved together to throw him overboard. He came to one of the corners of the ship in order to fall from it, and behold, a creature of the sea's creatures was watching him and lying in wait for him. He pushed to the other corner and found it likewise, until he had circled the vessel while it did not leave him. Then he knew that this was from Allah, so he threw himself toward it, and it swallowed him. It is related that it swallowed him only after he had fallen into the water. It is also related that Allah revealed to the fish: "I did not make Yunus a provision for you; rather, I made your belly a safe-keeping and a prison for him."

This is the meaning of ﴿"fasahama"﴾, that is, he drew lots (*qara'a*). Likewise Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi explained it. "Al-mudhad" means the one who is defeated and thrown down in a dispute, a drawing of lots, or a race, and from it comes the phrase *al-hujjah al-dahidah* (a refuted argument). "Al-mulim" means one who has done what he is blamed for; it is said: *alama al-rajul* means he entered into blame. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd explained it this way, and from it is the verse of the poet:

Foolishly you have blamed and reproached one who is not blameworthy,
And may the one who is not wise guide you before today.

Then Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, rescued him from the belly of the fish after a period, and people differed about the length of that period. One group said: after seven hours. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: after three days. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: after seven days. One group said: after fourteen days. Abu Malik and al-Suddi said: after forty days, and this is the statement of Ibn Jurayj, that it reached him. Allah, despite His previous power, made the cause of his rescue his glorification (*tasbih*). The people differed about this. Ibn Jubayr said: it is his saying in the belly of the fish: "Glory be to Allah." Another group said: rather it is glorification and voluntary prayer (*salat al-tatawwu'*). This group also differed. Qatadah, Ibn 'Abbas, and Abu al-'Aliyah said: his prayer in a time of ease benefited him in a time of hardship. A group of scholars said this. Al-Dahhak ibn Qays said from his pulpit: "Remember Allah in ease, and He will remember you in hardship. Indeed Yunus was a servant of Allah who remembered Him, so when hardship struck him, that benefited him." Then he recited this verse. And indeed, Pharaoh was a tyrant and transgressor; when drowning overtook him, he said, "I believe," and that did not benefit him. So remember Allah in ease, and He will remember you in hardship. Qatadah said regarding wisdom: "Indeed, good deeds lift up their doer when he stumbles; when he is thrown down, he finds something to lean on." Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "His glorification was prayer in the belly of the fish." It is related that he would raise the flesh of the fish with his hands and say: "O Lord, I will surely build You a mosque where no one has built one before me," and he would pray. Anas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed Yunus, when he called out in the darknesses, his call rose up to the Throne. The angels said: 'This is a weak voice from a place of strangeness.' Allah said: 'This is My servant Yunus,' so He answered his supplication." And he mentioned the hadith.

Ibn Jubayr said: the reference in His saying ﴿"of those who glorify"﴾ is to His saying: ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87]. People have written about this narrative what we have summarized, due to its lack of soundness. It is related that the fish carried him through all the seas until it cast him up in a place of two plains (*nasibayn*) on the side of Mosul, and Allah cast him onto an open tract of land, which is a wide, flat land with no trees or landmarks. From it is the verse of the poet:

I raised a foot whose stumbling I do not fear,
And I cast my garments on the open land of a town.

As for al-Suddi and Ibn 'Abbas in explaining His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿while he was ailing﴾: he was like a newborn child, a lump of flesh. Some of them said: he was like raw meat, except that nothing was lacking from his creation. So Allah revived him in the shade of the gourd-plant with the milk of a female gazelle, which would come to him in the morning and in the evening. It was also said: rather he would feed on the gourd-plant, finding from it all kinds of food and varieties of what he desired.

The people differed about *al-yaqtin* (the gourd). One group said: it is a tree we do not know, which Allah named *yaqtin*, and it is a word derived from *qatana*, meaning to remain in a place. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Muqatil said: *al-yaqtin* is everything that does not stand on a stalk of wood, such as herbs, squash, bitter gourd, watermelon, and the like, which die within their year. Something similar was narrated from Mujahid. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, and 'Amr ibn Maymun said: *al-yaqtin* is specifically the gourd (*qar'*). On these two statements, either His saying "a tree" is figurative (*tajawwuz*, a figure of speech), or He caused it to grow over him with a stalk, breaking the custom (*kharq li-l-'adah*), since in the speech of the Arabs the word "tree" is only used for what stands on a wooden stalk. Some people related that it was a gourd, which has several qualities: the coolness of its shade and its smoothness to the touch, the largeness of its leaves, and that flies do not approach it. Al-Naqqash related that when the water of gourd leaves is sprinkled in a place, no fly approaches it. The well-known meaning in the lexicon is that *al-yaqtin* is the gourd. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said in the story of Yunus, peace be upon him:

So He caused a gourd to grow over him by mercy
From Allah; had it not been for Allah, he would have been found exposed to the sun.

Yunus, peace be upon him, then recovered, was restored to health, and his body became sound, because gourd leaves are the most beneficial thing for one whose skin has peeled off, as Yunus's had. It is related that one day he was sleeping, and Allah dried up that gourd-plant. It was also said: He sent a termite upon it, and it cut its roots. Yunus woke up from the heat of the sun, and its matter grieved him greatly and he was distressed about it. Then Allah, may He be exalted, revealed to him: "O Yunus, are you distressed over the drying up of a gourd, and you were not distressed over the destruction of a hundred thousand or more who repented, so He accepted their repentance?"

(p-313)

﴿And indeed, Yunus was among the messengers.﴾ ﴿When he fled to the laden ship.﴾ ﴿Then he drew lots, and was among the losers.﴾ ﴿Then the fish swallowed him, and he was blameworthy.﴾ ﴿So had he not been of those who glorify Allah.﴾ ﴿He would have remained in its belly until the day they are resurrected.﴾ ﴿Then We cast him onto the open land while he was ailing.﴾ ﴿And We caused a gourd-plant to grow over him.﴾

He is Yunus ibn Matta, peace be upon him, from the Children of Israel. It is narrated that he was made a prophet at the age of twenty-eight, and he buckled under the burdens of prophethood as a rope-bridge (or a weak vessel) buckles under a load. His story has already been explained, but we will mention from it what is needed to understand these words.

It is narrated that Allah sent him to his people. He called them once, and they opposed him, so he threatened them with punishment. Allah informed him of its day, and Yunus set that time for them. Then, when his people saw the signs of the punishment before it reached them, they repented and believed, so Allah accepted their repentance and turned the punishment away from them. This was a test for Yunus, peace be upon him, and anger overtook Yunus. It is also related that it was among their custom that they would kill the liar if no clear proof was established for him. Yunus feared them, and in addition he was angry, so he fled to the ship. That is, he intended to escape and entered the sea. He expressed his escape with the word *ibaq* (running away from one's master), since he was a servant of Allah who fled without the permission of his master; this is the literal meaning of *ibaq*. "Al-Fulk" in this context is singular, and "al-mashhun" means the loaded (heavy-laden). (p-310) Here there is a narrative that has been omitted for brevity and conciseness.

It is related from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that when he was in the ship, it moved away and nearly sank and did not go on, while the other ships were moving to the right and left. The people of the ship said: "Among us there is one with a sin, and because of him Allah is holding us back." They said: "Let us draw lots." So they took for each person a lot, and said: "O Allah, let the lot of the sinner float, and let the lots of others sink." So the lot of Yunus floated. They did this three times, and each time the lot fell on him. They resolved together to throw him overboard. He came to one of the corners of the ship in order to fall from it, and behold, a creature of the sea's creatures was watching him and lying in wait for him. He pushed to the other corner and found it likewise, until he had circled the vessel while it did not leave him. Then he knew that this was from Allah, so he threw himself toward it, and it swallowed him. It is related that it swallowed him only after he had fallen into the water. It is also related that Allah revealed to the fish: "I did not make Yunus a provision for you; rather, I made your belly a safe-keeping and a prison for him."

This is the meaning of ﴿"fasahama"﴾, that is, he drew lots (*qara'a*). Likewise Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi explained it. "Al-mudhad" means the one who is defeated and thrown down in a dispute, a drawing of lots, or a race, and from it comes the phrase *al-hujjah al-dahidah* (a refuted argument). "Al-mulim" means one who has done what he is blamed for; it is said: *alama al-rajul* means he entered into blame. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd explained it this way, and from it is the verse of the poet:

Foolishly you have blamed and reproached one who is not blameworthy,
And may the one who is not wise guide you before today.

Then Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, rescued him from the belly of the fish after a period, and people differed about the length of that period. One group said: after seven hours. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: after three days. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: after seven days. One group said: after fourteen days. Abu Malik and al-Suddi said: after forty days, and this is the statement of Ibn Jurayj, that it reached him. Allah, despite His previous power, made the cause of his rescue his glorification (*tasbih*). The people differed about this. Ibn Jubayr said: it is his saying in the belly of the fish: "Glory be to Allah." Another group said: rather it is glorification and voluntary prayer (*salat al-tatawwu'*). This group also differed. Qatadah, Ibn 'Abbas, and Abu al-'Aliyah said: his prayer in a time of ease benefited him in a time of hardship. A group of scholars said this. Al-Dahhak ibn Qays said from his pulpit: "Remember Allah in ease, and He will remember you in hardship. Indeed Yunus was a servant of Allah who remembered Him, so when hardship struck him, that benefited him." Then he recited this verse. And indeed, Pharaoh was a tyrant and transgressor; when drowning overtook him, he said, "I believe," and that did not benefit him. So remember Allah in ease, and He will remember you in hardship. Qatadah said regarding wisdom: "Indeed, good deeds lift up their doer when he stumbles; when he is thrown down, he finds something to lean on." Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "His glorification was prayer in the belly of the fish." It is related that he would raise the flesh of the fish with his hands and say: "O Lord, I will surely build You a mosque where no one has built one before me," and he would pray. Anas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed Yunus, when he called out in the darknesses, his call rose up to the Throne. The angels said: 'This is a weak voice from a place of strangeness.' Allah said: 'This is My servant Yunus,' so He answered his supplication." And he mentioned the hadith.

Ibn Jubayr said: the reference in His saying ﴿"of those who glorify"﴾ is to His saying: ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87]. People have written about this narrative what we have summarized, due to its lack of soundness. It is related that the fish carried him through all the seas until it cast him up in a place of two plains (*nasibayn*) on the side of Mosul, and Allah cast him onto an open tract of land, which is a wide, flat land with no trees or landmarks. From it is the verse of the poet:

I raised a foot whose stumbling I do not fear,
And I cast my garments on the open land of a town.

As for al-Suddi and Ibn 'Abbas in explaining His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿while he was ailing﴾: he was like a newborn child, a lump of flesh. Some of them said: he was like raw meat, except that nothing was lacking from his creation. So Allah revived him in the shade of the gourd-plant with the milk of a female gazelle, which would come to him in the morning and in the evening. It was also said: rather he would feed on the gourd-plant, finding from it all kinds of food and varieties of what he desired.

The people differed about *al-yaqtin* (the gourd). One group said: it is a tree we do not know, which Allah named *yaqtin*, and it is a word derived from *qatana*, meaning to remain in a place. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Muqatil said: *al-yaqtin* is everything that does not stand on a stalk of wood, such as herbs, squash, bitter gourd, watermelon, and the like, which die within their year. Something similar was narrated from Mujahid. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, and 'Amr ibn Maymun said: *al-yaqtin* is specifically the gourd (*qar'*). On these two statements, either His saying "a tree" is figurative (*tajawwuz*, a figure of speech), or He caused it to grow over him with a stalk, breaking the custom (*kharq li-l-'adah*), since in the speech of the Arabs the word "tree" is only used for what stands on a wooden stalk. Some people related that it was a gourd, which has several qualities: the coolness of its shade and its smoothness to the touch, the largeness of its leaves, and that flies do not approach it. Al-Naqqash related that when the water of gourd leaves is sprinkled in a place, no fly approaches it. The well-known meaning in the lexicon is that *al-yaqtin* is the gourd. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said in the story of Yunus, peace be upon him:

So He caused a gourd to grow over him by mercy
From Allah; had it not been for Allah, he would have been found exposed to the sun.

Yunus, peace be upon him, then recovered, was restored to health, and his body became sound, because gourd leaves are the most beneficial thing for one whose skin has peeled off, as Yunus's had. It is related that one day he was sleeping, and Allah dried up that gourd-plant. It was also said: He sent a termite upon it, and it cut its roots. Yunus woke up from the heat of the sun, and its matter grieved him greatly and he was distressed about it. Then Allah, may He be exalted, revealed to him: "O Yunus, are you distressed over the drying up of a gourd, and you were not distressed over the destruction of a hundred thousand or more who repented, so He accepted their repentance?"

"Al-mudhad" means the one who is defeated and thrown down in a dispute, a drawing of lots, or a race, and from it comes the phrase *al-hujjah al-dahidah* (a refuted argument). "Al-mulim" means one who has done what he is blamed for; it is said: *alama al-rajul* means he entered into blame. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd explained it this way, and from it is the verse of the poet:

Foolishly you have blamed and reproached one who is not blameworthy,
And may the one who is not wise guide you before today.

Then Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, rescued him from the belly of the fish after a period, and people differed about the length of that period. One group said: after seven hours. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: after three days. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: after seven days. One group said: after fourteen days. Abu Malik and al-Suddi said: after forty days, and this is the statement of Ibn Jurayj, that it reached him. Allah, despite His previous power, made the cause of his rescue his glorification (*tasbih*). The people differed about this. Ibn Jubayr said: it is his saying in the belly of the fish: "Glory be to Allah." Another group said: rather it is glorification and voluntary prayer (*salat al-tatawwu'*). This group also differed. Qatadah, Ibn 'Abbas, and Abu al-'Aliyah said: his prayer in a time of ease benefited him in a time of hardship. A group of scholars said this. Al-Dahhak ibn Qays said from his pulpit: "Remember Allah in ease, and He will remember you in hardship. Indeed Yunus was a servant of Allah who remembered Him, so when hardship struck him, that benefited him." Then he recited this verse. And indeed, Pharaoh was a tyrant and transgressor; when drowning overtook him, he said, "I believe," and that did not benefit him. So remember Allah in ease, and He will remember you in hardship. Qatadah said regarding wisdom: "Indeed, good deeds lift up their doer when he stumbles; when he is thrown down, he finds something to lean on." Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "His glorification was prayer in the belly of the fish." It is related that he would raise the flesh of the fish with his hands and say: "O Lord, I will surely build You a mosque where no one has built one before me," and he would pray. Anas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed Yunus, when he called out in the darknesses, his call rose up to the Throne. The angels said: 'This is a weak voice from a place of strangeness.' Allah said: 'This is My servant Yunus,' so He answered his supplication." And he mentioned the hadith.

Ibn Jubayr said: the reference in His saying ﴿"of those who glorify"﴾ is to His saying: ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87]. People have written about this narrative what we have summarized, due to its lack of soundness. It is related that the fish carried him through all the seas until it cast him up in a place of two plains (*nasibayn*) on the side of Mosul, and Allah cast him onto an open tract of land, which is a wide, flat land with no trees or landmarks. From it is the verse of the poet:

I raised a foot whose stumbling I do not fear,
And I cast my garments on the open land of a town.

As for al-Suddi and Ibn 'Abbas in explaining His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿while he was ailing﴾: he was like a newborn child, a lump of flesh. Some of them said: he was like raw meat, except that nothing was lacking from his creation. So Allah revived him in the shade of the gourd-plant with the milk of a female gazelle, which would come to him in the morning and in the evening. It was also said: rather he would feed on the gourd-plant, finding from it all kinds of food and varieties of what he desired.

The people differed about *al-yaqtin* (the gourd). One group said: it is a tree we do not know, which Allah named *yaqtin*, and it is a word derived from *qatana*, meaning to remain in a place. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Muqatil said: *al-yaqtin* is everything that does not stand on a stalk of wood, such as herbs, squash, bitter gourd, watermelon, and the like, which die within their year. Something similar was narrated from Mujahid. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, and 'Amr ibn Maymun said: *al-yaqtin* is specifically the gourd (*qar'*). On these two statements, either His saying "a tree" is figurative (*tajawwuz*, a figure of speech), or He caused it to grow over him with a stalk, breaking the custom (*kharq li-l-'adah*), since in the speech of the Arabs the word "tree" is only used for what stands on a wooden stalk. Some people related that it was a gourd, which has several qualities: the coolness of its shade and its smoothness to the touch, the largeness of its leaves, and that flies do not approach it. Al-Naqqash related that when the water of gourd leaves is sprinkled in a place, no fly approaches it. The well-known meaning in the lexicon is that *al-yaqtin* is the gourd. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said in the story of Yunus, peace be upon him:

So He caused a gourd to grow over him by mercy
From Allah; had it not been for Allah, he would have been found exposed to the sun.

Yunus, peace be upon him, then recovered, was restored to health, and his body became sound, because gourd leaves are the most beneficial thing for one whose skin has peeled off, as Yunus's had. It is related that one day he was sleeping, and Allah dried up that gourd-plant. It was also said: He sent a termite upon it, and it cut its roots. Yunus woke up from the heat of the sun, and its matter grieved him greatly and he was distressed about it. Then Allah, may He be exalted, revealed to him: "O Yunus, are you distressed over the drying up of a gourd, and you were not distressed over the destruction of a hundred thousand or more who repented, so He accepted their repentance?"

(p-313)

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 37, verse 147–157:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more.﴾ ﴿So they believed, and We gave them enjoyment for a time.﴾ ﴿So ask them: "Does your Lord have daughters while they have sons?"﴾ ﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾ ﴿Unquestionably, it is from their own fabrication that they say:﴾ ﴿"Allah has begotten," and indeed they are liars.﴾ ﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ ﴿What is wrong with you? How do you judge?﴾ ﴿Will you not remember?﴾ ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ ﴿Then bring your Book, if you are truthful.﴾

The majority said: This mission "to a hundred thousand" belongs to his first mission, from which he fled (abaqa) after it, and Allah, exalted is He, mentioned it at the end of the stories as a reminder of his mission. What indicates this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they believed, and We gave them enjoyment for a time﴾. The enjoyment given to that community is what angered Yunus, peace be upon him, until he fled. Qatadah and Ibn 'Abbas also said: this mission was another one after he had been cast out into the open (bil-'ara'), and it was to the people of Nineveh, from the direction of Mosul.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with him, read "wa-yazidun" with a waw, while the majority read: ﴿"aw yazidun"﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "aw" here means "bal" (rather), and they were a hundred and thirty thousand. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said, from the Prophet ﷺ: "They were a hundred and twenty thousand." Ibn Jubayr said: they were a hundred and seventy thousand. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he read: "bal yazidun" (rather they exceed). A group said that "aw" here means the waw (and). Another group said it is for indefiniteness addressed to the listener, as you say: "It is no concern of yours; I give so-and-so a dinar or a thousand dinars." A similar usage is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You have no part in the matter, whether He turns to them or punishes them, for indeed they are wrongdoers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 128]. This meaning, however, has little firmness in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿or they exceed﴾. Al-Mubarrad and many of the Basrans said: the meaning is according to human perception and estimation, i.e., whoever saw them would say: they are a hundred thousand or more.

It is narrated concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they believed, and We gave them enjoyment for a time﴾, that they went out with the children and the young of animals, separated them from their mothers, wailed and cried out, and sincerely repented, so Allah lifted the punishment from them. The enjoyment here is with life, and the "hin" (time) refers to their predetermined lifespans in eternity; this was said by Qatadah and al-Suddi. Ibn Abi 'Abla read: [hatta hin] (until a time). In His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they believed, and We gave them enjoyment for a time﴾ there is an example for Quraysh: that is, if they believe, they will be safe, as occurred for those people. From here the speech and discourse shifted smoothly to them with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So ask them﴾, since their pronoun refers to what is implied in the meaning of their mention.

"Istifta'" means asking, and here it carries the sense of rebuke and reproach, for their saying a lie against Allah and their making daughters for Allah, exalted is He far above that. He also commanded him to question them, in a manner of reproach too: did they witness that the angels are females, so that they may rightly make that claim?

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed about a group among them whose falsehood and lying reached the point of saying: "Allah begot the angels, because He married among the chiefs of the jinn." This, as it is narrated, was a group of the Banu Mudlij.

The majority read ﴿'asTafa﴾ with an initial hamza (alif qat') which is interrogative, and this is by way of confirmation and rebuke for their attributing to Him the choice of what is lesser in their view. Nafi', in the transmission of Isma'il, read [istafa] with a connected alif, as a declarative statement, as if relating the monstrousness of their saying; Isma'il narrated it from Abu Ja'far, and Shayba.

Then He confirmed, rebuked, and drew attention to reminder and reflection, and asked about the proof and argument, by way of confirmation and of demanding from them support through a book or a matter that would make their truthfulness evident. The majority read "tadhakkarun" with the dhal and kaf both doubled (shaddah), while Talhah ibn Musarrif read it with the dhal sukun and the kaf damma, lightly.

In His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they believed, and We gave them enjoyment for a time﴾ there is an example for Quraysh: that is, if they believe, they will be safe, as occurred for those people. From here the speech and discourse shifted smoothly to them with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So ask them﴾, since their pronoun refers to what is implied in the meaning of their mention.

"Istifta'" means asking, and here it carries the sense of rebuke and reproach, for their saying a lie against Allah and their making daughters for Allah, exalted is He far above that. He also commanded him to question them, in a manner of reproach too: did they witness that the angels are females, so that they may rightly make that claim?

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed about a group among them whose falsehood and lying reached the point of saying: "Allah begot the angels, because He married among the chiefs of the jinn." This, as it is narrated, was a group of the Banu Mudlij.

The majority read ﴿'asTafa﴾ with an initial hamza (alif qat') which is interrogative, and this is by way of confirmation and rebuke for their attributing to Him the choice of what is lesser in their view. Nafi', in the transmission of Isma'il, read [istafa] with a connected alif, as a declarative statement, as if relating the monstrousness of their saying; Isma'il narrated it from Abu Ja'far, and Shayba.

Then He confirmed, rebuked, and drew attention to reminder and reflection, and asked about the proof and argument, by way of confirmation and of demanding from them support through a book or a matter that would make their truthfulness evident. The majority read "tadhakkarun" with the dhal and kaf both doubled (shaddah), while Talhah ibn Musarrif read it with the dhal sukun and the kaf damma, lightly.

(p-315) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship. The pronoun in His saying, ﴿"And they have made"﴾, refers to a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said in the book of al-Tabari: some of them said, "Allah and Iblis are brothers." Mujahid said: a people said to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, "Allah, exalted is He, married among the chieftains of the jinn." Some of them said: "The angels are His daughters." So "al-jinnah" in this last view refers to the angels; they were named so because they are concealed (mustajinnah), that is, hidden.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿"And the jinn have certainly known that they will surely be brought forward"﴾: whoever takes "al-jinnah" to mean the devils (shayatin) takes the mark of the verb in ﴿"they have known"﴾, and the pronoun in ﴿"that they"﴾, as referring to them. That is: they made the devils to be not from Allah, while the devils know the opposite of that, that they will be brought forward before the command of Allah, His reward and His punishment. Whoever takes "al-jinnah" to mean the angels takes the pronoun in "that they" to refer to the speakers of this statement. That is: the angels know that these disbelievers will be brought forward to the reward and punishment of Allah. These two views may overlap.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, declared Himself far above what people attribute to Him and what is not fitting for Him. From this He excepted the chosen servants, because they describe Him with His most beautiful attributes. A group said: He excepted them from His saying "will surely be brought forward"; and this is valid according to the view of the one who holds that "al-jinnah" means the angels.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿"Indeed, you and what you worship"﴾, its meaning is: say to them, O Muhammad: "Indeed, you and your idols cannot lead anyone astray through them, except him for whom the decree has already preceded and destiny has embraced, that he will burn in the Hereafter in the Fire. This is how Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan explained it. Ibn al-Zubayr said from the pulpit: "Allah is the Guide and the Misleader." And "man" is in a position of accusative governed by "fatinin." The majority read ﴿"ṣāli al-jaḥīm"﴾ with the kasra on the lam of "ṣāli," the yaʾ being dropped for the idafa (annexation). Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "ṣālu al-jaḥīm" with a damma on the lam. The grammarians have conflicting views about its meaning, and the strongest of them is that it is "ṣāluna," the nun being dropped for the idafa, then the waw dropped due to the meeting of two unvowelled letters, and the plural form came after the singular form, so it is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿"And among them are those who listen"﴾ [Yunus: 42], since "man," which is among the words that carry ambiguity and are used to refer to both singular and plural, [is treated this way].

Then He related the saying of the angels: ﴿"And there is none of us except that he has a known station."﴾ This supports that by "al-jinnah" He meant the angels, as if He said: "And the angels have known such-and-such, and our saying is such-and-such." The sense of the speech is: "There is none of us an angel except..." The Prophet ﷺ was narrated by ʿA’isha, may Allah be pleased with her, as saying: "Indeed, in the heaven there is not a spot the size of a footstep except that upon it is the forehead of an angel or his feet." Ibn Mas'ud said: "And indeed, none of us except that he has a known station."

It is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that when the prayer was established he would turn his face to the people and say to them: "Straighten your rows and align them, for Allah only wants you to follow the guidance of the angels, for they say: ﴿And indeed, we are the ones who line up﴾ ﴿And indeed, we are the ones who glorify﴾." Then he would see the rows straightened, and at that point he would turn and say takbir. Al-Zahrawi said: It has been said that the Muslims have lined up in rows only since this verse was revealed, and no one among the people of other religions lines up except the Muslims.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned the statement of some of the disbelievers. Qatada, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: before the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ they said, "If we had a book, or a messenger had come to us, we would have been among the most God-fearing servants of Allah and the most sincere of them." But when Muhammad came to them, they disbelieved, and so they deserved painful punishment.

The rest of the surah is clear.

He said: 'So I did when I recited to Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, and he said to me what I said to you, and he said that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said to him the same, and he said: "Say: I have warned you with the warning of the messengers.
